units.title: Sentence structure & word order
units.intro: English is S-V-O. Tigrinya is S-O-V, so keep the verb as a middle anchor and use an overt copula.

cards.title: S-V-O vs S-O-V
rule: English declarative order is **Subject–Verb–Object**.
Tigrinya is **Subject–Object–Verb**; putting the English verb last is a common L1 error.
Keep the main verb as a **middle anchor** after the subject.

examples.text: The guard locked the gate at midnight.
The guard the gate locked at midnight.
examples.fix: The guard locked the gate at midnight.

examples.text: Locked the guard the gate.
examples.fix: The guard locked the gate.

cards.title: Why the verb goes in the middle
body: In English the position of a word shows its job. The noun **before** the verb is the doer (subject) and the noun **after** the verb is the receiver (object): *The dog bit the boy* and *The boy bit the dog* mean different things only because of word order.
Tigrinya puts the verb at the end (literally "I letter read"). If you translate word for word you get **S-O-V** English, which is wrong: ✗ *I the letter read* → **I read the letter**.

A quick test: underline the subject, then check that the very next part is the verb (with its auxiliaries): *The students **have finished** their project.* Time and place phrases usually go at the end: *We met our teacher **in the market yesterday**.*
Questions are the main exception: an auxiliary comes before the subject (*Did you finish?*), but the main verb still comes before the object.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "The guard the gate locked at midnight."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** English declarative order is **Subject–Verb–Object**.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "The guard the gate locked at midnight." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "The guard locked the gate at midnight."
**Check:** Tigrinya is **Subject–Object–Verb**; putting the English verb last is a common L1 error.
**Same pattern:** "Locked the guard the gate." → "The guard locked the gate."

cards.answer: The guard locked the gate at midnight.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the sentence with correct word order.

options.A: Our team the regional final won last year.
options.B: Won our team the regional final last year.
options.C: Our team won the regional final last year.
options.D: Our team last year the regional final won.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The subject is "Our team" and the verb is "won".

**Step 2:** The object "the regional final" follows the verb; the time phrase goes last.

**Step 3:** Only the first option is S-V-O.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "The boy kicked the ball." What is the object?
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The object receives the action and normally comes after the verb.

**Step 2:** "the ball" is what was kicked.

**Step 3:** "the boy" is the subject; "kicked" is the verb.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which sentence shows an L1 (Tigrinya) word-order error?

options.A: Every morning my mother makes injera.
options.B: My mother injera every morning makes.
options.D: My mother makes injera every morning.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Tigrinya puts the verb last (S-O-V).

**Step 2:** "My mother injera every morning makes" copies that order.

**Step 3:** The other sentences keep the verb after the subject.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Copula and clause boundaries
rule: English needs an overt copula (*is/are/was/were*) between subject and complement.
Do not join two independent clauses with only a comma (comma splice).
Use a full stop, semicolon, or a conjunction (*and/but/so/because*).

examples.text: She is a teacher.
She a teacher.
examples.fix: She is a teacher.

examples.text: It rained; therefore we stayed in.

cards.title: Linking verbs and sentence boundaries
body: A **copula** (linking verb) connects the subject to a description: *be, become, seem, look, feel*. Tigrinya can drop or attach the copula, but English always needs it: ✗ *She a nurse* → **She is a nurse**; ✗ *The soup hot* → **The soup is hot**.
A **clause boundary** is where one complete idea ends. Two complete ideas cannot be joined by a comma alone (a *comma splice*): ✗ *I was hungry, I ate*.

Four correct ways to fix a comma splice: (1) full stop: *I was hungry. I ate.* (2) semicolon: *I was hungry; I ate.* (3) comma + FANBOYS: *I was hungry, so I ate.* (4) subordinator: *Because I was hungry, I ate.*
Watch long subjects: *The books on the top shelf **are** old* – the copula agrees with "books", not "shelf".

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She a teacher."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** English needs an overt copula (*is/are/was/were*) between subject and complement.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She a teacher." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She is a teacher."
**Check:** Do not join two independent clauses with only a comma (comma splice).

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Use S-V-O, place the copula after the subject, and close clause boundaries without comma splices.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which sentence is correct?

options.A: The weather very is hot in Massawa.
options.B: Very hot the weather in Massawa.
options.C: The weather very hot in Massawa.
options.D: The weather is very hot in Massawa.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** A subject + adjective needs a copula.

**Step 2:** "is" must come between "The weather" and "very hot".

**Step 3:** The other sentences omit it or misplace it.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: How can you correct "He missed the bus, he was late"?

options.A: He missed, the bus he was late.
options.B: He missed the bus, he late.
options.C: He missed the bus, so he was late.
options.D: He missed the bus he was late.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The original is a comma splice: two independent clauses joined by a comma.

**Step 2:** Adding "so" after the comma joins them correctly and shows result.

**Step 3:** Option D removes the comma but is still a run-on sentence.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the sentence without an error.

options.A: I was tired; however, I finished the work.
options.B: I tired, but I finished the work.
options.C: I was tired however, I finished the work.
options.D: I was tired, however I finished the work.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** "however" joins clauses with a semicolon before and a comma after.

**Step 2:** Option B is a comma splice; C misses the copula "was"; D puts the comma in the wrong place.

**Step 3:** Only the first option is correct.

**Tip:** Find the subject, then make sure a finite verb follows it. Never leave the verb at the end (S-O-V) and never join two full sentences with only a comma.

Identify the sentence that contains a copula verb

options.A: The security guard the main gate locked at midnight.
options.B: The security guard locked the main gate at midnight.
options.C: At midnight the security guard the main gate locked.
options.D: Locked the security guard the main gate at midnight.

why: Answer B: The security guard locked the main gate at midnight.
English requires a strict Subject-Verb-Object ($$\text{S-V-O}$$) pattern. The subject is 'The security guard', the verb is 'locked', and the direct object is 'the main gate'.

Option A and Option C place the verb ('locked') at the end of the clause, which is an $$\text{S-O-V}$$ pattern typical of Tigrinya grammar (ሓላው ሰላም ማዕጾ ዓጸዎ) and represents a common L1 transfer error. Option D incorrectly places the verb before the subject without an auxiliary in a declarative statement.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

Choose the sentence that correctly manages sentenc

options.A: She is an excellent English teacher.
options.B: They are very proud of their exam results.
options.C: My brother a hardworking farmer in the village.
options.D: We were delighted to receive your letter.

why: Answer C: My brother a hardworking farmer in the village.
Every English sentence expressing a state of being requires an explicit copula verb ('is', 'are', 'was', 'were') between the subject and the predicate nominative.

In Option C, the copula verb 'is' is completely missing. In Tigrinya, the copula can sometimes be omitted or structurally merged, leading students to translate "ሓወይ ኣብቲ ዓዲ ትጉህ ሓረስታይ [እዩ]" directly as "My brother a hardworking farmer..." without including the essential English copula 'is'.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

Complete the sentence with the correct word order:

options.A: The rain was heavy, we decided to stay indoors.
options.B: The rain was heavy we decided to stay indoors.
options.C: The rain was heavy; therefore, we decided to stay indoors.
options.D: Because the rain was heavy, so we decided to stay indoors.

why: Answer C: The rain was heavy; therefore, we decided to stay indoors.

A comma splice occurs when two independent clauses are joined with only a comma. Option A is a comma splice. Option B is a run-on sentence. Option C uses a semicolon and a conjunctive adverb ('therefore'), which is structurally perfect.

Option D is a double-conjunction error ('Because... so...'). Tigrinya speakers often use both because they translate morphological markers like "ስለዝ-... ስለዚ..." directly into English. Option C correctly separates the clauses.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

Which of the following ditransitive sentences is g

options.A: yesterday welcomed the new students warmly
options.B: warmly welcomed the new students yesterday
options.C: welcomed yesterday warmly the new students
options.D: the new students welcomed warmly yesterday

why: Answer B: warmly welcomed the new students yesterday

English adverbs of manner ('warmly') usually precede the main verb or follow the object. Adverbs of time ('yesterday') belong at the end of the sentence. The correct structure is: Subject ('The school principal') + Adverb of Manner ('warmly') + Verb ('welcomed') + Object ('the new students') + Adverb of Time ('yesterday').

Option D shows $$\text{S-O-V}$$ word order. Option A places the time adverb ('yesterday') between the subject and the verb, which is acceptable in Tigrinya but highly irregular and awkward in English unless formatted as a fronted adverbial.

Identify the sentence that has a word order error

options.A: The grandmother told a beautiful story her grandchildren.
options.B: The grandmother told to her grandchildren a beautiful story.
options.C: The grandmother told her grandchildren a beautiful story.
options.D: The grandmother her grandchildren a beautiful story told.

why: Answer C: The grandmother told her grandchildren a beautiful story.

Ditransitive verbs ('tell', 'give', 'buy') can take two structures: $$\text{S} + \text{V} + \text{Indirect Object (IO)} + \text{Direct Object (DO)}$$ OR $$\text{S} + \text{V} + \text{DO} + \text{to/for} + \text{IO}$$.

Option C follows the $$\text{S-V-IO-DO}$$ pattern ('her grandchildren' is IO, 'a beautiful story' is DO). Option A lacks the preposition 'to' which is required if DO comes before IO. Option D is an $$\text{S-O-V}$$ trap.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

Which of the following sentences exhibits the corr

options.A: He is not a member of the organizing committee.
options.B: They are not ready to take the national examination.
options.C: She is a doctor not in this public hospital.
options.D: We are not satisfied with the current classroom conditions.

why: Answer C: She is a doctor not in this public hospital.
In English, negative copular sentences follow the structure: $$\text{Subject} + \text{Copula} + \text{not} + \text{Complement}$$.

Option C places 'not' after the predicate noun phrase ('a doctor not...'). In Tigrinya, negation is prefixed and suffixed to the copula at the end (ንሳ ኣብዚ ዶክተር ኣይኮነትን), which can lead students to misplace the negative particle in English.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

options.A: Although the storm damaged many homes, the community rebuilt quickly.
options.B: The storm damaged many homes, but the community rebuilt quickly.
options.C: The storm damaged many homes the community rebuilt quickly.
options.D: The storm damaged many homes; the community rebuilt quickly.

why: Answer C: The storm damaged many homes the community rebuilt quickly.
A run-on sentence occurs when two independent clauses are joined without any punctuation or coordinating conjunctions.

Option C strings 'The storm damaged many homes' and 'the community rebuilt quickly' together with zero punctuation. Tigrinya speakers, used to inflectional markers on verbs for clausal relationships, often overlook the strict English requirement for punctuation boundaries or conjunctions.

similar.q: Identify the sentence that contains a copula verb

options.A: The athlete ran in the stadium gracefully this morning.
options.B: The athlete ran gracefully this morning in the stadium.
options.C: The athlete ran gracefully in the stadium this morning.
options.D: This morning the athlete ran in the stadium gracefully.

why: Answer C: The athlete ran gracefully in the stadium this morning.
When multiple adverbials modify a single verb, English follows the sequence: Manner (How) $$\rightarrow$$ Place (Where) $$\rightarrow$$ Time (When).

In Option C: 'gracefully' (Manner), 'in the stadium' (Place), and 'this morning' (Time) are correctly sequenced ($$\text{M} \rightarrow \text{P} \rightarrow \text{T}$$). Other options violate this standard order, which is a frequent target in matric grammar tasks.

options.A: The adverb of time 'last week' is at the end.
options.B: There is a double subject ('My cousin' and 'he').
options.D: The direct object 'a new car' is misplaced.

why: Answer B: There is a double subject ('My cousin' and 'he').
In English, a noun subject must not be followed immediately by its corresponding pronoun subject in the same clause. This creates a redundant double subject.

In Tigrinya, verbs are conjugated with pronominal suffixes that match the subject (e.g., ወዲ ሓወይ መኪና ዓዲጉ - where the verb contains the subject marker). Direct translation often causes students to state the subject and then immediately repeat it with a pronoun ('My cousin he...').

why: Answer B: Where did you buy that beautiful traditional dress?
English Wh-questions with active verbs require subject-auxiliary inversion: $$\text{Wh-word} + \text{Auxiliary Verb (do/does/did)} + \text{Subject} + \text{Base Verb} + \text{Object}$$.

Option B correctly inverts 'did' and 'you'. Option A and Option C are common L1 transfer errors where the speaker maintains standard declarative word order ($$\text{Wh-word} + \text{Subject} + \text{Verb}$$).

units.title: Subject–verb agreement
units.intro: The verb must agree with its true subject in number, even when phrases come between them.

cards.title: Basic agreement
rule: Singular subject → singular verb: *The exam **starts** at eight.*
Plural subject → plural verb: *The exams **start** at eight.*
A phrase between subject and verb does not change agreement: *The box of books **is** heavy.*

examples.text: The list of names is long.
The list of names are long.
examples.fix: The list of names is long.

examples.text: My friends are ready.

cards.title: Finding the real subject
body: The verb must agree with the **head noun** of the subject, which is often far from the verb. Cross out phrases that come between them: *The box ✗ *of oranges* **is** heavy; The students ✗ *in the last row* **are** quiet.*
Relative clauses do the same: *The man ✗ *who sells vegetables* **lives** next door.*
In present simple, a singular third-person subject (he, she, it, one person or thing) takes **-s**: *The bus **leaves** at seven.* Plural subjects take the base form: *The buses **leave** at seven.*
Two subjects joined by **and** are plural: *Aster and Ruth **are** cousins* – except when they form one idea: *Bread and butter **is** my breakfast.*

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "The list of names are long."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Singular subject → singular verb: *The exam **starts** at eight.*
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "The list of names are long." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "The list of names is long."
**Check:** Plural subject → plural verb: *The exams **start** at eight.*

cards.answer: The list of names is long.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The box of pens ____ on the desk.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The head noun is "box" (singular).

**Step 2:** "of pens" is a prepositional phrase and does not change agreement.

**Step 3:** So: is.

**Tip:** Find the head noun of the subject. Ignore phrases like "of the students", "along with", "as well as". With either/or and neither/nor, agree with the nearer noun.

units.title: Modals & semi-modals
units.intro: Modals (*can, must, should, might…*) express ability, obligation, advice and possibility without *to*.

cards.title: Core modals
rule: **must / have to** = obligation; **should / ought to** = advice.
**can / could** = ability or permission; **may / might** = possibility.
Modal + bare infinitive: *You should revise.*

examples.text: You should revise tonight.
You should to revise tonight.
examples.fix: You should revise tonight.

examples.text: It might rain later.

cards.title: Choosing a modal by meaning
body: Modals add attitude to a verb. Always ask *what is the speaker's meaning?* – **obligation** (must, have to), **no obligation** (don't have to, needn't), **prohibition** (mustn't), **advice** (should, ought to), **ability** (can, could), **permission** (can, may), **possibility** (may, might, could).
**must** usually shows the speaker's own feeling or a rule; **have to** often shows an outside rule: *I must study tonight* vs *We have to wear uniform.* In the past both become **had to**.
Grammar of modals: no -s (*she can*), no to (*you should go*), questions by inversion (*Can you help?*), negatives with not (*mustn't, can't*).

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "You should to revise tonight."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **must / have to** = obligation; **should / ought to** = advice.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "You should to revise tonight." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "You should revise tonight."
**Check:** **can / could** = ability or permission; **may / might** = possibility.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Almaz might be working late tonight.

options.A: Definitely, she will be working late tonight.
options.B: Certainly, she will be working late tonight.
options.C: She is unlikely to work late tonight.
options.D: Perhaps she will be working late tonight.
options.E: She will never be working late tonight.

cards.why:
**Meaning:** The modal verb **might** expresses a possibility, not a certainty. 
**Step 1:** Choices A and B imply 100% certainty (Definitely/Certainly), which is wrong.
**Step 2:** Choices C and E imply it won't happen, which is wrong.
**Step 3:** Choice D uses "Perhaps" (ምናልባት), which is the correct synonym for 'might'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Elsa: Do you have to go to the party now? 
Abraham: I _______ go but I don’t think I will.
cards.why: The speaker says 'I don't think I will', which indicates uncertainty or a weak possibility. 'Might' is used to express a weak possibility that something will happen.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: All the students _______ take Model Examinations this week. They won’t be given later on.
cards.why: The second sentence ('They won’t be given later on') implies a strict requirement or obligation. 'Must' is used to express strong obligation.

cards.title: Perfect modals
rule: **must have + V3** = logical conclusion about the past.
**should have + V3** = past advice / regret.
**could have + V3** = past possibility that did not happen.

examples.text: She must have left early.
She must left early.
examples.fix: She must have left early.

examples.text: You should have told me.

cards.title: Perfect modals in context
body: Perfect modals look back at the past: **modal + have + past participle**.
**must have** = I'm sure it happened (*The streets are wet – it must have rained*). **can't/couldn't have** = I'm sure it didn't happen. **may/might/could have** = perhaps it happened.
**should have** = it was the right thing but it didn't happen (regret or criticism): *You should have revised.* **shouldn't have** = it happened, but it was wrong.
**could have** can also mean a chance that was not taken: *We could have won if we had trained.* **needn't have** = done, but unnecessary.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She must left early."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** **must have + V3** = logical conclusion about the past.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She must left early." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She must have left early."
**Check:** **should have + V3** = past advice / regret.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: After a modal use the bare infinitive: must go, not must to go.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Choose the modal for meaning (obligation vs advice vs possibility) and keep the bare verb after it.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Every child should __________ his or her parents and other people.
cards.why: **Rule:** After modal verbs like *should, must, can, could, will,* we always use the **bare infinitive** (base form of the verb without 'to'). Therefore, "should respect" is correct.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: It is so amazing how a single tower can ___19___ so astonishing.
cards.why: After the modal verb 'can', the base form of the verb (without 'to' or '-s') must be used. Therefore, 'look' is correct.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "The window is broken and there is a football on the floor. Someone ____ it."
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The evidence makes the speaker sure about a past event.

**Step 2:** Strong deduction about the past: must have + past participle.

**Step 3:** "should have" would mean it was the right thing to do.

**Tip:** Choose the modal by meaning: obligation, advice, ability, permission, possibility or deduction. For the past, use modal + have + past participle.

glossary.meaning: helping verb of mood: can, must, should…

tips.text: After a modal use the bare infinitive: must go, not must to go.

units.title: Active and passive voice
units.intro: Passive = be + past participle. Use it when the receiver matters more than the doer.

cards.title: Forming the passive
rule: Active S-V-O → Passive: object becomes subject + **be + V3** (+ by-agent).
Tense of be matches the active tense: writes→is written; wrote→was written.
Do not omit be: *The bridge was built*, not *The bridge built*.

examples.text: The report was written yesterday.
The report written yesterday.
examples.fix: The report was written yesterday.

examples.text: The gate is locked every night.

cards.title: From active to passive in three steps
body: **Step 1:** Take the object of the active sentence and make it the new subject: *The students planted **the trees*** → ***The trees** ...*
**Step 2:** Put "be" in the same tense as the active verb and add the past participle: planted (past simple) → **were planted**.
**Step 3:** Add *by + agent* only if it is important: *The trees were planted (by the students).*
Typical L1 trap: Tigrinya passives are formed on the verb itself (*ተሰሪሑ*), so learners drop "be": ✗ *The school built in 1990* → **The school was built in 1990**.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "The report written yesterday."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Active S-V-O → Passive: object becomes subject + **be + V3** (+ by-agent).
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "The report written yesterday." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "The report was written yesterday."
**Check:** Tense of be matches the active tense: writes→is written; wrote→was written.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The World Cup 2022 matches were being televised all over the world. (Choose the correct active form)

options.A: All over the world, the World Cup 2022 matches were being televised.
options.B: Television channels televised the World Cup 2022 matches all over the world.
options.C: Television channels were televising the World Cup 2022 matches all over the world.
options.D: All over the world, the World Cup 2022 football matches were televised.
options.E: The World Cup 2022 matches televised all over the world.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Identify the tense. "Were being televised" is **Past Continuous Passive**.
**Step 2:** The active form must also be in Past Continuous (**was/were + verb-ing**).
**Step 3:** "Television channels were televising" is the correct active conversion.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Which of the following is the **passive voice form** of the sentence in italics?

*My mother advised me not to go out alone.*

options.A: I am advised not to go out alone.
options.B: I had been advised not to go out alone.
options.C: I advised my mother not to out alone.
options.D: I was advised not to go out alone.
options.E: I always advise not to go out alone.

cards.why: The active sentence is in the Past Simple ('advised'). To convert to passive, 'me' becomes 'I', and we use 'was/were + V3'. Thus, 'I was advised' is correct.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the passive form of "The workers repaired the road."

options.A: The workers were repaired by the road.
options.B: The road was repair by the workers.
options.C: The road was repaired by the workers.
options.D: The road repaired by the workers.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** The object "the road" becomes the subject.

**Step 2:** Past simple active → was + V3 (repaired).

**Step 3:** Option B drops "be"; C lacks -ed; D reverses the meaning.

**Tip:** Passive = correct tense of "be" + past participle (V3). Keep the tense of the active verb in the form of "be", and never drop "be".

cards.title: Progressive and perfect passives
rule: Progressive: *is being cleaned*.
Perfect: *has been signed*.
Future: *will be completed* / *will have been completed*.

examples.text: The room is being painted.
The room is been painted.
examples.fix: The room is being painted. / has been painted.

examples.text: The form has been submitted.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "The room is been painted."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Progressive: *is being cleaned*.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "The room is been painted." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "The room is being painted. / has been painted."
**Check:** Perfect: *has been signed*.

cards.answer: The room is being painted. / has been painted.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: If the subject is inanimate and cannot perform the action, expect a passive.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Form passives with the correct be-tense + V3; do not drop be (L1 trap).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Someone is painting Mr. Munir’s office.

options.A: Mr. Munir’s office is being painted now.
options.C: Mr. Munir’s office have been painted.
options.D: Mr. Munir’s office is been painted now.
options.E: Mr. Munir’s office is being painted by no one.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** Identify the tense. 'is painting' is Present Continuous.
**Step 2:** The passive structure for Present Continuous is 'am/is/are + being + V3'.
**Step 3:** 'Mr. Munir's office' is singular, so we use 'is being painted'.
**Result:** Option A.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I hate the colour with _______ they painted this room.
cards.why: The relative pronoun refers to 'the colour', which is a thing. 'Which' is the correct pronoun for things/objects.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Which of the following is the **active voice form** of the sentence in italics?

*The prisoners had been severely tortured before they were sent to the islands by them.*

options.A: They had severely tortured the prisoners before they sent them to the islands.
options.B: They have severely tortured the prisoners before they have sent them to the islands.
options.C: They severely tortured the prisoners after they sent them to the islands.
options.D: They have severely tortured the prisoners before they had sent them to the islands.
options.E: They severely tortured the prisoners before they had sent them to the islands.

cards.why: The passive sentence is in the Past Perfect ('had been tortured'). To convert to active, the subject 'them' becomes 'They', and the verb becomes 'had tortured'. The second part 'were sent' (Past Simple Passive) becomes 'sent' (Past Simple Active). Choice A is correct.

questions.q: The official report on the regional economic development ________ by the committee before the deadline last night.
questions.label: 1. The official report on the regional economic development ___

similar.q: The official report on the regional economic devel
A massive amount of money ________ currently _____

why: The subject 'The official report' is inanimate and cannot perform the action of submitting. This requires the passive voice. The time-marker 'last night' indicates the Simple Past tense, requiring the past passive form ($$\text{was/were} + \text{V}_3$$).

Students often choose the active form 'submitted' (Option A) due to direct translation, or 'has been submitted' (Option C), which is present perfect and cannot be paired with the definite past time-marker 'last night'.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: A massive amount of money ________ currently ________ to fund the construction of the new school library.
questions.label: 2. A massive amount of money ________ currently ________ to fun

similar.q: A massive amount of money ________ currently _____
The high school teacher ________ a beautiful tradi

why: The subject is 'A massive amount of money' (singular and inanimate), requiring the passive voice. The time-marker 'currently' indicates an action in progress, requiring the Present Progressive Passive ($$\text{is/are} + \text{being} + \text{V}_3$$).
Students often choose 'is raising' (Option A) because they confuse active and passive progressive forms. Since 'money' cannot raise itself, the passive 'is being raised' (Option B) is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: The high school teacher ________ a beautiful traditional gift by the students on her graduation day.
questions.label: 3. The high school teacher ________ a beautiful traditional gif

similar.q: The high school teacher ________ a beautiful tradi
The national examination papers ________ by next F

why: This is a double-object passive where the Indirect Object 'The high school teacher' is placed in the subject position: $$\text{IO} + \text{be} + \text{V}_3 + \text{DO}$$.

Students often choose 'gave' (Option A) because they see a person as the subject and assume the active voice. However, the context shows she received the gift, requiring the passive form 'was given' (Option B).
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: The national examination papers ________ by next Friday afternoon, according to the official schedule.
questions.label: 4. The national examination papers ________ by next Friday afte

similar.q: The national examination papers ________ by next F
The legendary king of Axum ________ to have built

why: Answer B: will have been printed

The inanimate subject 'examination papers' requires the passive voice. The time-marker 'by next Friday' indicates a future point of completion, requiring the Future Perfect Passive ($$\text{will have been} + \text{V}_3$$).

Students often see 'next Friday' and choose active 'will print' (Option A) or active future perfect 'will have printed' (Option D). Because papers cannot print themselves, the passive 'will have been printed' (Option B) is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: The legendary king of Axum ________ to have built several stone obelisks during his reign.
questions.label: 5. The legendary king of Axum ________ to have built several st

similar.q: The legendary king of Axum ________ to have built
A prestigious academic scholarship ________ to Daw

why: This is an impersonal passive reporting structure using the subject-infinitive pattern: $$\text{Subject} + \text{be} + \text{V}_3 + \text{to-infinitive}$$.

Students often choose active 'believes' (Option A) or progressive 'is believing' (Option D). Since the king does not believe himself, but people believe *about* him, the passive 'is believed' (Option B) is required.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: A prestigious academic scholarship ________ to Dawit because of his outstanding ESSLCE results.
questions.label: 6. A prestigious academic scholarship ________ to Dawit because

similar.q: A prestigious academic scholarship ________ to Daw
The official report on the regional economic devel

why: This is a double-object passive where the Direct Object 'A prestigious academic scholarship' is the subject: $$\text{DO} + \text{be} + \text{V}_3 + \text{to} + \text{IO}$$.
Students often choose 'awarded' (Option B) because they assume the active past tense. However, a scholarship cannot award itself, making the passive 'was awarded' (Option A) correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: The historic church in the village ________ in the 14th century, but historians are still researching its origin.
questions.label: 7. The historic church in the village ________ in the 14th cent

similar.q: The official report on the regional economic devel

why: The subject 'The historic church' is inanimate. The definite past time-marker 'in the 14th century' strictly requires the Past Simple passive ($$\text{was/were} + \text{V}_3$$).
Students often choose 'has been built' (Option A) because they see it as a permanent present state. Definite historical dates require the simple past passive 'was built' (Option B).
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: It ________ that the ancient city of Adulis was a prosperous port for international trade.
questions.label: 8. It ________ that the ancient city of Adulis was a prosperous

similar.q: A massive amount of money ________ currently _____

why: This is an impersonal passive reporting structure using the introductory 'It' pattern: $$\text{It} + \text{be} + \text{V}_3 + \text{that-clause}$$.
Students often choose active 'reports' (Option A) or 'reported' (Option C) because they translate directly from Tigrinya. The formal English reporting structure requires 'It is reported' (Option B).
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: Several modern research laboratories ________ in our school since the regional budget was increased.
questions.label: 9. Several modern research laboratories ________ in our school

similar.q: The high school teacher ________ a beautiful tradi

why: The time-marker 'since' indicates an action that started in the past and continues to the present, requiring the Present Perfect Passive ($$\text{have/has been} + \text{V}_3$$).

Students often choose active 'have established' (Option A) or simple past passive 'were established' (Option C). Because the laboratories were established by someone, and 'since' requires a perfect tense, Option B is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: While the laboratory experiments ________ by the science students, the principal walked in to inspect the rooms.
questions.label: 10. While the laboratory experiments ________ by the science stu

similar.q: The national examination papers ________ by next F

why: 'While' introduces an ongoing background action in the past, requiring the Past Continuous. The subject 'experiments' is inanimate, requiring the Past Progressive Passive ($$\text{was/were being} + \text{V}_3$$).
Students often choose active 'were conducting' (Option A). However, experiments cannot conduct themselves, so the passive 'were being conducted' (Option B) is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

Future passive: will be + past participle.

units.title: Reported speech
units.intro: Reported speech shifts tense and pronouns when the reporting verb is past.

cards.title: Backshift basics
rule: Direct: *“I am ready,” she said.* → Reported: *She said (that) she was ready.*
will → would; can → could; have done → had done.
*tell* needs a person object: *He told me to wait.*

examples.text: She said she was tired.
She said she is tired yesterday.
examples.fix: She said she was tired.

examples.text: He told me to wait.

cards.title: The backshift table
body: When the reporting verb is past (*said, told, asked*), move each tense one step back: present simple → past simple; present continuous → past continuous; present perfect / past simple → past perfect; will → would; can → could; may → might; must → had to.
Change time and place words: now → then; today → that day; tomorrow → the next day; yesterday → the day before; here → there; this → that; ago → before.
No backshift is needed when the fact is still true or the reporting verb is present: *She says she **is** tired; He said the Earth **goes** round the sun.*

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She said she is tired yesterday."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Direct: *“I am ready,” she said.* → Reported: *She said (that) she was ready.*
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She said she is tired yesterday." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She said she was tired."
**Check:** will → would; can → could; have done → had done.

cards.title: Forms and examples
head: Direct
Reported
rows: She told me to stay there.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: He said, ”I had seen the film before.”

options.A: He said that he has seen the film by now.
options.B: He said that he has seen the film before.
options.C: He said that he had seen the film before.
options.D: He ordered that to see the film.

cards.why: When the direct speech is already in the Past Perfect ('had seen'), it remains in the Past Perfect in indirect speech. Note: Option B uses 'has seen' (Present Perfect), which is incorrect. Option C is the correct conversion.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: He said that he had to go at once.

options.A: The boy said, ”I will have to go at once.”
options.B: The boy said, ”I must to go at once.”
options.C: The boy said, ”I have to go at once.”
options.D: The boy said, ”I had to go at once.”
options.E: The boy said, ”I want to go at once.”

cards.why: When converting indirect speech with 'had to' back to direct speech, 'had to' usually changes back to 'have to' or 'must'. Option B is grammatically incorrect ('must to' is wrong). Therefore, 'I have to go at once' is the correct direct form.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: They said that they were going to church. (Change to Direct Speech)

options.A: They said, “They were going to church.”
options.B: They said, “We were going to church.”
options.C: They said, “We are going to church.”
options.D: They said, “They are going to church

cards.why: To change from indirect to direct speech: the past continuous 'were going' changes back to present continuous 'are going', and the pronoun 'they' (referring to the speakers) changes to 'we'.

cards.title: Questions and commands
rule: Yes/No: *asked if/whether* + clause (no do-support).
Wh-questions: keep the wh-word; use statement order.
Commands: *told/asked + object + to-infinitive*.

examples.text: She asked if I was ready.
She asked was I ready.
examples.fix: She asked if I was ready.

examples.text: He told us to sit down.

cards.title: Reporting questions and commands
body: **Yes/no questions:** asked + if/whether + statement order: *"Are you hungry?" → She asked if I was hungry.*
**Wh-questions:** keep the wh-word, use statement order and no do/does/did: *"Where do you live?" → He asked where I lived.*
**Commands and requests:** tell/ask/order + person + (not) to-infinitive: *"Close the door." → She told me to close the door. "Don't shout." → He asked us not to shout.*
Other useful reporting verbs: advise, remind, warn, invite, refuse, promise – each with its own pattern (*He promised to come; She warned me not to touch it*).

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She asked was I ready."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Yes/No: *asked if/whether* + clause (no do-support).
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She asked was I ready." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She asked if I was ready."
**Check:** Wh-questions: keep the wh-word; use statement order.

cards.answer: She asked if I was ready.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: Backshift: present→past, past→past perfect, will→would; keep place/time words consistent.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Use told + person, said (that)…; adjust tense when the reporting verb is past.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She said, "Where have you been?"

options.A: She said that where were you.
options.B: She asked me where I was.
options.C: She said to me that where have I had.
options.D: She asked me where was I.
options.E: She asked me where I had been.

cards.why: The Present Perfect **'have been'** changes to Past Perfect **'had been'**. In indirect questions, the subject ('I') comes before the auxiliary verb ('had').

options.B: She asked them whether they have seen a scorpion.

units.title: Conditionals & wish
units.intro: Match if-clause and result tenses: 0/1 real, 2 unreal present, 3 unreal past, mixed for past→present.

cards.title: Types 0–3
rule: 0: If + present, present (facts).
1: If + present, will + V (real future).
2: If + past, would + V (unreal now); prefer *were*.
3: If + past perfect, would have + V3 (unreal past).

examples.text: If it rains, we will stay in.
If it will rain, we will stay in.
examples.fix: If it rains, we will stay in.

examples.text: If I were you, I would apply.

cards.title: Choosing the right conditional
body: Ask two questions: **Is it real or unreal?** and **Is it about the present/future or the past?**
**Real, always true → Type 0:** *If you press this, the light comes on.* **Real, possible future → Type 1:** *If it rains, we'll stay in.*
**Unreal present/future → Type 2:** *If I had wings, I would fly* (I don't have wings). **Unreal past → Type 3:** *If she had trained, she would have won* (she didn't train).
The if-clause can come second without a comma: *We'll stay in if it rains.* "Unless" = if not; "provided / as long as" = only if.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "If it will rain, we will stay in."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** 0: If + present, present (facts).
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "If it will rain, we will stay in." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "If it rains, we will stay in."
**Check:** 1: If + present, will + V (real future).

cards.answer: If it rains, we will stay in.

cards.title: Forms and examples
head: Type
Form
rows: If + had + V3, would have + V3

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If you ____ ice, it melts.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** This is a general fact: type 0.

**Step 2:** Type 0 uses the present simple in both clauses.

**Step 3:** So: If you heat ice, it melts.

**Tip:** Identify the conditional type from the verb forms: 0 (present, present), 1 (present, will), 2 (past, would), 3 (past perfect, would have). Never put "would" in the if-clause.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If I ____ the answer, I would tell you.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "would tell" shows an unreal present situation: type 2.

**Step 2:** The if-clause takes the past simple.

**Step 3:** So: If I knew the answer ...

**Tip:** Identify the conditional type from the verb forms: 0 (present, present), 1 (present, will), 2 (past, would), 3 (past perfect, would have). Never put "would" in the if-clause.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If she had asked me, I ____ her.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "had asked" shows type 3 (unreal past).

**Step 2:** The main clause takes would have + past participle.

**Step 3:** So: I would have helped her.

**Tip:** Identify the conditional type from the verb forms: 0 (present, present), 1 (present, will), 2 (past, would), 3 (past perfect, would have). Never put "would" in the if-clause.

cards.title: Mixed conditionals and wish
rule: Past cause → present result: *If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.*
Wish + past = present regret; wish + past perfect = past regret.
Inverted forms: *Had I known…*, *Were I you…*, *Should you need…*.

examples.text: If she had trained, she would be fitter now.
I wish I had prepared yesterday.
I wish I prepared yesterday.
examples.fix: I wish I had prepared yesterday.

cards.title: Expressing wishes and regrets
body: **wish + past simple** = I want the present to be different: *I wish I **had** more time* (I don't have enough).
**wish + past perfect** = regret about the past: *I wish I **had studied** harder* (I didn't).
**wish + would** = complaint about someone's behaviour: *I wish you **would** stop talking.*
"If only" is a stronger form of wish: *If only I had listened!*

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "I wish I prepared yesterday."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** Past cause → present result: *If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.*
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "I wish I prepared yesterday." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "I wish I had prepared yesterday."
**Check:** Wish + past = present regret; wish + past perfect = past regret.

cards.answer: I wish I had prepared yesterday.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: Never put would in the if-clause of type 2/3; use were for formal type 2.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Zero/first for facts and real futures; second/third for unreal present/past; wish uses unreal past forms.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I wish I knew Ali's mobile phone number.

options.C: I don't know the number and I regret this.

cards.why:
**Analysis:** The structure "I wish + Past Simple" is used to express a regret about a present situation. It means the opposite of the current reality. 
**Reality:** I **do not know** the number right now, and I am unhappy about it. Choice C correctly captures both the fact and the feeling.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: If they had waited another month, they could probably __________ a better price for their house.
cards.why: This is a **Third Conditional** sentence (unreal past). The structure is: If + Past Perfect, Subject + could/would + have + Past Participle. Therefore, 'have got' is the correct completion.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: My mother _______ everything before she left for the training programme.
cards.why:
The sentence describes two actions in the past: preparing everything and leaving. When one past action happens before another past action, we use the **Past Perfect Tense** (had + past participle) for the earlier action. 

1. First Action: Preparing (Past Perfect)
2. Second Action: Leaving (Simple Past)

glossary.meaning: if and result refer to different times

tips.text: Never put would in the if-clause of type 2/3; use were for formal type 2.

Students are often confused by the lack of 'if' at the beginning of the sentence. Recognizing 'Had... arrived' as an inverted conditional makes the correct choice 'would have saved' (Option B) clear.

Students often choose 'have' (Option A) because they see 'now'. However, because the wish is about an unreal present situation (I wish I had time, but I don't), the Past Simple 'had' (Option B) is correct.

Students often blindly choose 'would not have been' (Option A) because they see 'hadn't eaten' in the 'if' clause. However, the present result marker 'today' requires the mixed conditional form 'would not be' (Option B).

why: The conjunction 'Unless' means 'if... not' and carries a negative meaning. The First Conditional formula requires: $$\text{Unless} + \text{Present Simple}, \text{will not} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$.

Because *unless* is already negative, you cannot use a negative verb like 'don't start' (Option A) in the *unless* clause. This double-negative trap is highly tested on exams. Option B 'start' is correct.

Students often choose 'Had' (Option A) or 'Were' (Option B). However, 'Had' is for third conditional inversion and 'Were' is for second conditional. 'Should' (Option C) is the correct auxiliary for first conditional inversion.

units.title: Gerunds, infinitives & participles
units.intro: Some verbs take -ing, some take to-infinitive; prepositions take -ing.

cards.title: Verb patterns
rule: enjoy/avoid/suggest/finish + -ing.
want/decide/hope/plan + to-infinitive.
stop + -ing = quit; stop + to-V = pause in order to.

examples.text: She enjoys reading.
She enjoys to read.
examples.fix: She enjoys reading.

examples.text: We stopped to rest.

cards.title: Common verb patterns to memorise
body: **Verb + -ing:** enjoy, avoid, finish, mind, suggest, consider, keep, practise, deny, admit, imagine, risk.
**Verb + to-infinitive:** want, decide, hope, plan, agree, refuse, promise, offer, manage, afford, learn, expect.
**Verb + object + to-infinitive:** ask, tell, advise, allow, encourage, warn (*She advised me to rest*). **Verb + object + bare infinitive:** let, make (*They made us wait*).
**Change of meaning:** remember/forget + -ing (past memory) vs + to (future duty); stop + -ing (quit) vs + to (in order to); try + -ing (experiment) vs + to (make an effort).

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "She enjoys to read."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** enjoy/avoid/suggest/finish + -ing.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "She enjoys to read." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "She enjoys reading."
**Check:** want/decide/hope/plan + to-infinitive.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She said that the letter was personal and wouldn’t let me _____ it.
cards.why: The verb 'let' is followed by an object and then the bare infinitive (verb without 'to').

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She finished ____ her essay at midnight.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "finish" is followed by a gerund (-ing).

**Step 2:** So: finished writing.

**Step 3:** "to write" is wrong after finish.

**Tip:** Learn verb patterns as chunks: enjoy + -ing, decide + to, look forward to + -ing. After a preposition always use -ing.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "Don't forget ____ the lights before you leave."
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "forget + to-infinitive" refers to an action you need to do in the future.

**Step 2:** "forget + -ing" refers to a past memory.

**Step 3:** Here the action is in the future: to switch off.

**Tip:** Learn verb patterns as chunks: enjoy + -ing, decide + to, look forward to + -ing. After a preposition always use -ing.

cards.title: Adjective + infinitive; preposition + -ing
rule: easy/hard/important + to-infinitive.
good at / interested in / before + -ing.
look forward to + -ing (*to* is a preposition here).

examples.text: It is important to listen.
She is interested in studying history.
I look forward to meet you.
examples.fix: I look forward to meeting you.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "I look forward to meet you."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** easy/hard/important + to-infinitive.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "I look forward to meet you." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "I look forward to meeting you."
**Check:** good at / interested in / before + -ing.

cards.answer: I look forward to meeting you.

cards.title: Memory tip
body: After a preposition always use a gerund: interested in learning.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Memorise high-frequency patterns; stop + -ing ≠ stop + to-infinitive.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I am accustomed______late at night.
cards.why: The phrase 'be accustomed to' is followed by a gerund (-ing form). Here, 'to' is a preposition, not part of an infinitive.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In spite of all the disadvantages, students are very interested __________ video games.
cards.why: The adjective 'interested' is always followed by the preposition **in** (e.g., interested in music, interested in sports).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: He is afraid ____ alone at night.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The fixed pattern is "afraid of + -ing / noun".

**Step 2:** After the preposition "of" the verb takes -ing.

**Step 3:** So: afraid of walking.

**Tip:** Learn verb patterns as chunks: enjoy + -ing, decide + to, look forward to + -ing. After a preposition always use -ing.

tips.text: After a preposition always use a gerund: interested in learning.

questions.q: The driver of the school bus managed to avoid ________ the pedestrian on the narrow mountain road.
questions.label: 1. The driver of the school bus managed to avoid ________ the p

similar.q: The driver of the school bus managed to avoid ____
We are extremely looking forward to ________ the h

why: The lexical verb 'avoid' belongs to the category of verbs that must strictly govern a gerund: $$\text{avoid} + \text{Gerund}$$.
Students often choose 'to hit' (Option A) due to direct translation of infinitival thoughts. Option B 'hitting' is the correct gerund form required by 'avoid'.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: We are extremely looking forward to ________ the historical obelisks of Axum during our school holidays.
questions.label: 2. We are extremely looking forward to ________ the historical

similar.q: We are extremely looking forward to ________ the h
I clearly remember ________ the laboratory door, b

why: In the phrasal verb 'look forward to', 'to' functions as a preposition, not an infinitive marker. Therefore, it must strictly be followed by a gerund ($$\text{look forward to} + \text{V-ing}$$).

Students almost always fall for the trap of choosing 'visit' (Option A) or 'to visit' (Option C) because they see 'to'. This is a high-frequency prepositional trap on national exams. Option B is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

While walking to the school library, he stopped __

why: The context 'but I should double-check to be sure' shows that the locking happened in the past, and the speaker now has a memory of it. This past memory requires a gerund: $$\text{remember} + \text{Gerund}$$.
Students often confuse 'remember to lock' (future duty) with 'remember locking' (past memory). Since the locking was already performed, 'locking' (Option B) is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

Despite the heavy rain and road blockages, we mana

why: The context shows that the speaker interrupted his walk *in order to* buy bread. This purpose or reason requires a to-infinitive: $$\text{stop} + \text{to-infinitive}$$.
Students often confuse 'stop to buy' (pause to do) with 'stop buying' (quit the habit). Since he paused his walk to perform the action, 'to buy' (Option B) is correct.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

She is highly interested in ________ biochemistry

why: The verb 'manage' strictly governs a to-infinitive: $$\text{manage} + \text{to-infinitive}$$.
Students often choose 'arriving' (Option A) thinking it fits the progressive sense of the sentence. Only the to-infinitive 'to arrive' (Option B) is grammatically correct after 'manage'.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.label: 6. She is highly interested in ________ biochemistry when she j

why: The adjective phrase 'interested in' contains the preposition 'in'. All prepositions must be followed strictly by gerunds: $$\text{Preposition} + \text{Gerund}$$.
Students are often tempted to choose 'to study' (Option B) because they translate "ክተጽንዕ" directly. Prepositional phrases strictly require 'studying' (Option A).
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: ________ his final examination papers, Dawit quietly walked out of the hall to rest.
questions.label: 7. ________ his final examination papers, Dawit quietly walked

similar.q: The driver of the school bus managed to avoid ____

why: The sentence describes two past actions in chronological sequence: first, finishing the exam, and second, walking out. This requires a perfect participle clause: $$\text{Having} + \text{V}_3 \dots$$.
Option A 'Finishing' implies the actions were happening at the exact same time, which is logically incorrect. Option B 'Having finished' correctly indicates the prior completion of the first action.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: ________ down the narrow street, the old university library suddenly appeared on our left.
questions.label: 8. ________ down the narrow street, the old university library

similar.q: We are extremely looking forward to ________ the h

why: Answer C: While we were walking
If we use 'Walking' (Option A), the subject of the main clause ('the old university library') becomes the logical subject of walking, creating a dangling modifier error (the library cannot walk).

Students often choose 'Walking' (Option A) because they fail to check subject-matching. Option C 'While we were walking' correctly provides an explicit subject ('we'), resolving the dangling modifier.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.q: The candidate strongly objected to ________ the additional registration fee for the examination.
questions.label: 9. The candidate strongly objected to ________ the additional r

similar.q: I clearly remember ________ the laboratory door, b

why: In 'object to', 'to' is a preposition. Therefore, it must be followed by a gerund ($$\text{object to} + \text{V-ing}$$).
Students see 'to' and choose 'pay' (Option A) or 'to pay' (Option C), falling into the infinitive trap. The phrasal verb requires 'paying' (Option B).
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence, find the clue word, then test each option.

questions.label: 10. The suspect persistently denied ________ the secure universi

Students often choose 'to enter' (Option A) due to L1 translation. Only the gerund 'entering' (Option B) is correct after 'deny'.

units.title: Cohesive devices
units.intro: Connectors show addition, contrast, cause and purpose — and each class has its own grammar.

cards.title: Contrast and purpose
rule: although/even though + S + V.
despite/in spite of + noun / V-ing.
so that + S + modal; in order to + Vbase.

examples.text: Although he studied, he failed.
Despite he studied, he failed.
examples.fix: Despite studying, he failed. / Although he studied, he failed.

examples.text: He revised so that he could pass.

cards.title: Connectors and the structures that follow them
body: **Contrast:** although / even though / though + clause; despite / in spite of + noun or -ing; however / nevertheless + new clause (after ; or .); whereas / while for direct comparison.
**Purpose:** to / in order to / so as to + base verb; so that + clause (often with can/could/would).
**Result:** so (after a comma); therefore / consequently / as a result (after ; or .); such + noun + that; so + adjective + that.
**Addition:** and; moreover / furthermore / in addition (after ; or .); not only ... but also.

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "Despite he studied, he failed."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** although/even though + S + V.
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "Despite he studied, he failed." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "Despite studying, he failed. / Although he studied, he failed."
**Check:** despite/in spite of + noun / V-ing.

cards.answer: Despite studying, he failed. / Although he studied, he failed.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She bought the dress __________ it was expensive.
cards.why: The sentence shows a contrast (concession). 'Although' is followed by a full clause (subject + verb: 'it was expensive'). 'Despite' and 'In spite of' would require a noun phrase.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The team was at full strength despite the injury of one of its players.

options.A: The team wasn't complete because one of its players was injured.
options.B: The team was at full strength in spite of the injury of one of its players.
options.C: The team was at full strength because of the injury of one of its players.
options.D: The team wasn't at full strength although none of its players was injured.
options.E: The team was at full strength despite the injury of many of its players.

cards.why:
**Analysis:** The original sentence uses "despite" to show a contrast. 
**Step 1:** "In spite of" is the exact synonym for "despite".
**Step 2:** Choice B maintains the exact meaning: even though someone was injured, the team was still strong. 
**Step 3:** Choice A says it was not complete (wrong), Choice C says injury caused the strength (wrong).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: He ought to look forward to achieving his goal __________ the temporarily existing difficulties.
cards.why: The word **'despite'** is a preposition used to show contrast. It is followed by a noun phrase ('the temporarily existing difficulties'). 'Even though' would require a full clause.

cards.title: Conjunctive adverbs
rule: therefore / however / moreover join two clauses with a semicolon before and a comma after: *It rained; however, we played.*
Do not write Because… so… or Although… but… (double conjunction).
Match meaning: therefore=result, however=contrast, moreover=addition.

examples.text: It flooded; therefore classes stopped.
Although she tried, but she failed.
examples.fix: Although she tried, she failed.

examples.text: The roads were blocked; however, buses ran.

cards.title: Punctuating conjunctive adverbs
body: Conjunctive adverbs (however, therefore, moreover, consequently, nevertheless, otherwise) are **not** conjunctions. They cannot join two clauses with only a comma.
Correct patterns: *It rained; **however**, we played.* or *It rained. **However**, we played.* or inside the clause: *We, **however**, played.*
Wrong: ✗ *It rained, however we played.* (comma splice).
Use only one connector per link: ✗ *Although it rained, but we played* → *Although it rained, we played.*

cards.title: Find and correct the error
cards.problem: Find and correct the error: "Although she tried, but she failed."

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the rule.** therefore / however / moreover join two clauses with a semicolon before and a comma after: *It rained; however, we played.*
**Step 2: Test the sentence.** "Although she tried, but she failed." breaks this rule.
**Step 3: Correct it.** "Although she tried, she failed."
**Check:** Do not write Because… so… or Although… but… (double conjunction).

cards.title: Common mistakes
head: Wrong
Right
Why
rows: Although he was late… / Despite being late…

cards.title: Memory tip
body: although + clause; despite + noun/gerund; so that + clause; in order to + base verb.

cards.title: Unit summary
body: Pick the connector for the logic and for the structure that follows the blank.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the clause which is connected correctly.

options.A: Because he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.B: Despite he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.C: In spite of he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.D: Since he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.
options.E: Although he'd never tried it before, he was very good at it.

cards.why: The sentence shows a contrast (never tried it vs. very good at it). 'Although' is a conjunction followed by a full clause (subject + verb). 'Despite' and 'In spite of' must be followed by a noun or gerund, not a clause.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the correctly punctuated sentence.

options.A: The exam was difficult; nevertheless, most students passed.
options.B: The exam was difficult, nevertheless most students passed.
options.C: The exam was difficult nevertheless, most students passed.
options.D: The exam was difficult; nevertheless most students, passed.

cards.why:
**Step 1:** "nevertheless" is a conjunctive adverb.

**Step 2:** It needs a semicolon (or full stop) before it and a comma after it.

**Step 3:** Only the first option follows this pattern.

**Tip:** Check both meaning (contrast, result, addition, purpose) and structure: although + clause; despite + noun/-ing; so that + clause; in order to + verb; ; however, + clause.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: "She practised every day; ____, she won the competition."
cards.why:
**Step 1:** Winning was a result of practising every day.

**Step 2:** "as a result" introduces a consequence.

**Step 3:** The others show contrast, example or condition.

units.title: Nouns, Pluralization
units.intro: Grammar from Study Notes: Nouns, Pluralization & Quantifiers.

cards.title: Nouns, Pluralization
rule: Definition: Nouns, Pluralization & Quantifiers (ስማት፡ ምብዛሕ ቁጽርን መለክዕታትን) refers to the syntactic and semantic rules governing the classification of nouns into countable or uncountable entities, the morphological modifications required for pluralization, and the precise application of modifying determiners (quantifiers and articles) to express amount or specificity.

English nouns are strictly divided into countable (ዝቝጸሩ) and uncountable (ዘይቝጸሩ) categories, a distinction that dictates both subject-verb agreement and modifier selection. Countable nouns represent individual, separable units (e.g., *student, chair, exam*) that can take both singular and plural forms. Uncountable nouns, on the other hand, represent mass entities, abstract concepts, or materials (e.g., *information, water, advice, furniture, luggage, progress*) that structurally exist only in the singular form and cannot be directly counted without partitive units (e.g., *a piece of advice, two items of luggage*). A major source of L1 interference (ኣሉታዊ ጽልዋ ቀዳማይ ቋንቋ) arises because many English uncountable nouns are treated as countable in Tigrinya. For instance, "ሓበሬታ" (information) or "ምኽሪ" (advice) are easily pluralized in Tigrinya ("ሓበሬታታት", "ምኽርታት"), leading students to incorrectly write "informations" or "advices" on exams.

Pluralization mechanics in English are not limited to the standard formula of adding $$\text{Noun} + \text{-s/es/ies}$$. Matriculation exams heavily test irregular plurals (ዘይስሩዓት ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ), particularly those derived from Latin or Greek roots. Examples include $$\text{criterion} \rightarrow \text{criteria}$$, $$\text{phenomenon} \rightarrow \text{phenomena}$$, $$\text{crisis} \rightarrow \text{crises}$$, and $$\text{focus} \rightarrow \text{foci}$$. Furthermore, English has zero-plural nouns (ዘይቅየሩ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ) such as *sheep, deer, species,* and *series*, which retain identical singular and plural spellings. Tigrinya speakers, accustomed to systematic broken plurals (ሰባር ብዙሕ - e.g., "መጽሓፍ" to "መጻሕፍቲ") or suffixation ("-ታት"), frequently struggle to identify these irregular patterns, often choosing incorrect plural forms like "phenomenons" or "sheeps" on grammar tests.

body: Definition: Nouns, Pluralization & Quantifiers (ስማት፡ ምብዛሕ ቁጽርን መለክዕታትን) refers to the syntactic and semantic rules governing the classification of nouns into countable or uncountable entities, the morphological modifications required for pluralization, and the precise application of modifying determiners (quantifiers and articles) to express amount or specificity.

English nouns are strictly divided into countable (ዝቝጸሩ) and uncountable (ዘይቝጸሩ) categories, a distinction that dictates both subject-verb agreement and modifier selection. Countable nouns represent individual, separable units (e.g., *student, chair, exam*) that can take both singular and plural forms. Uncountable nouns, on the other hand, represent mass entities, abstract concepts, or materials (e.g., *information, water, advice, furniture, luggage, progress*) that structurally exist only in the singular form and cannot be directly counted without partitive units (e.g., *a piece of advice, two items of luggage*). A major source of L1 interference (ኣሉታዊ ጽልዋ ቀዳማይ ቋንቋ) arises because many English uncountable nouns are treated as countable in Tigrinya. For instance, "ሓበሬታ" (information) or "ምኽሪ" (advice) are easily pluralized in Tigrinya ("ሓበሬታታት", "ምኽርታት"), leading students to incorrectly write "informations" or "advices" on exams.

Pluralization mechanics in English are not limited to the standard formula of adding $$\text{Noun} + \text{-s/es/ies}$$. Matriculation exams heavily test irregular plurals (ዘይስሩዓት ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ), particularly those derived from Latin or Greek roots. Examples include $$\text{criterion} \rightarrow \text{criteria}$$, $$\text{phenomenon} \rightarrow \text{phenomena}$$, $$\text{crisis} \rightarrow \text{crises}$$, and $$\text{focus} \rightarrow \text{foci}$$. Furthermore, English has zero-plural nouns (ዘይቅየሩ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ) such as *sheep, deer, species,* and *series*, which retain identical singular and plural spellings. Tigrinya speakers, accustomed to systematic broken plurals (ሰባር ብዙሕ - e.g., "መጽሓፍ" to "መጻሕፍቲ") or suffixation ("-ታት"), frequently struggle to identify these irregular patterns, often choosing incorrect plural forms like "phenomenons" or "sheeps" on grammar tests.

Abstract nouns (ረቂቕ ወይ ስነ-ሓሳባዊ ስማት - e.g., *knowledge, honesty, patience, courage*) represent another critical area of exam focus. These nouns represent non-physical concepts and are structurally uncountable, meaning they cannot be paired with the indefinite article *a/an* or pluralized ($$\text{Abstract Noun} \neq \text{Plural}$$). In academic English, they are often used with zero article when making general statements (e.g., "Honesty is the best policy"). L1 transfer errors frequently lead students to insert the definite article "the" inappropriately (e.g., "The honesty is important") because Tigrinya often nominalizes abstract concepts using definite markers or contextual demonstratives.

cards.title: Form tricky plurals
cards.problem: Write the plural of: box, baby, knife, child, sheep, potato, criterion.

steps.text: **Step 1: -s, -x, -ch, -sh, -z → add -es.** box → boxes.
**Step 2: consonant + y → -ies.** baby → babies.
**Step 3: many -f/-fe → -ves.** knife → knives.
**Step 4: irregular forms must be learnt.** child → children; sheep → sheep (no change).
**Step 5: some -o words take -es.** potato → potatoes.
**Step 6: Greek/Latin words.** criterion → criteria.
**Tip:** check the last letters first, then think of irregular and borrowed words.

cards.answer: boxes, babies, knives, children, sheep, potatoes, criteria.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The manager rejected the proposal because he felt that ________ details were provided to support the budget.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The blank modifies the noun 'details'. 'Details' is a plural countable noun (indicated by the '-s' ending).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Uncountable quantifiers like 'little' and 'a little' cannot modify plural countable nouns. 'Too few' is the correct quantifier for countable nouns in a negative context. Tigrinya speakers often conflate 'few' and 'little' as both translate to 'ውሑድ' or 'ቅሩብ'.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Details' (ዝርዝር ሓበሬታታት) ዝቝጸር ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ (countable plural) ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ምስኡ ክኸይድ ዝኽእል መለክዕ 'few' ጥራይ እዩ። 'Little' ንዘይቝጸሩ ስማት ጥራይ ስለ ዝገልጽ ክንጥቀመሉ ኣይንኽእልን። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'too few' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following sentences contains a pluralization error?

options.A: The laboratory analyzed various natural phenomena.
options.B: We must establish clear criteria for the scholarship.
options.C: The school board discussed several educational crisises.
options.D: The shepherd guided the sheep down the mountain.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
'Crisis' is a noun of Greek origin. Its plural form is 'crises', not 'crisises'.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
National exams frequently test irregular non-English plurals. Students often try to apply the regular '-es' rule to words ending in '-is' (like crisis, oasis, thesis), producing incorrect forms like 'crisises' (Option C).

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ናይ ግሪኽን ላቲንን መበቆል ዘለዎም ስማት ፍሉይ ናይ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ ምስራዕ ኣለዎም። 'Crisis' (ቅልውላው) ዝብል ስም ኣብ ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ ክቕየር ከሎ 'crises' ይኸውን እምበር 'crisises' ኣይበሃልን። ስለዚ Option C ጌጋ ዘለዎ ምሉእ ሓሳብ እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: We have ____ time before the bus leaves, so let's have a quick tea.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "time" here is uncountable.

**Step 2:** "a little" means a small but sufficient amount.

**Step 3:** "a few" and "many" are for countable nouns; "few" is also countable.

**Tip:** Decide if the noun is countable or uncountable first. Countable: many, few, a few, a number of. Uncountable: much, little, a little, an amount of.

cards.title: Pronouns, Case Concord
rule: Pronouns, Case Concord & Gender Agreement

Definition: Pronouns, Case Concord & Gender Agreement (ተውላጠ ስማት፡ ስምምዕ ኬዝን ጾታን) refers to the grammatical rules governing the substitution of nouns with pronouns, ensuring precise coordination in case (subjective, objective, possessive), grammatical number (singular, plural), and gender (masculine, feminine, neuter).

English personal pronouns are categorized into three distinct syntactic cases: subjective ($$\text{Subject Case}$$ - *I, you, he, she, it, we, they*), objective ($$\text{Object Case}$$ - *me, you, him, her, it, us, them*), and possessive ($$\text{Possessive Case}$$ - *my/mine, your/yours, his, her/hers, its, our/ours, their/theirs*). Unlike Tigrinya, where the case of a pronoun is often marked by attaching prefixes or suffixes directly to the pronoun base, English uses entirely different word forms to signal a pronoun's grammatical role in a sentence. This leads to a common case concord error (ጌጋ ስምምዕ ኬዝ) in compound constructions. For example, Tigrinya speakers often write "The director invited Aster and I" instead of the correct "The director invited Aster and me" because they translate both subjects and objects similarly without isolating the post-verbal objective slot.

examples.text: She goes to school every day.
She go to school every day.
examples.fix: She goes to school every day.
