body: Pronouns, Case Concord & Gender Agreement

Definition: Pronouns, Case Concord & Gender Agreement (ተውላጠ ስማት፡ ስምምዕ ኬዝን ጾታን) refers to the grammatical rules governing the substitution of nouns with pronouns, ensuring precise coordination in case (subjective, objective, possessive), grammatical number (singular, plural), and gender (masculine, feminine, neuter).

English personal pronouns are categorized into three distinct syntactic cases: subjective ($$\text{Subject Case}$$ - *I, you, he, she, it, we, they*), objective ($$\text{Object Case}$$ - *me, you, him, her, it, us, them*), and possessive ($$\text{Possessive Case}$$ - *my/mine, your/yours, his, her/hers, its, our/ours, their/theirs*). Unlike Tigrinya, where the case of a pronoun is often marked by attaching prefixes or suffixes directly to the pronoun base, English uses entirely different word forms to signal a pronoun's grammatical role in a sentence. This leads to a common case concord error (ጌጋ ስምምዕ ኬዝ) in compound constructions. For example, Tigrinya speakers often write "The director invited Aster and I" instead of the correct "The director invited Aster and me" because they translate both subjects and objects similarly without isolating the post-verbal objective slot.

Gender agreement (ጾታዊ ስምምዕ) presents a major challenge for Tigrinya speakers due to structural differences in how inanimate objects are treated. In Tigrinya, there is no neuter (ጾታ ኣልቦ) pronoun equivalent to the English "it". Every noun in Tigrinya is grammatically classified as either masculine or feminine. For instance, a car ("መኪና") or the sun ("ጸሓይ") is treated as feminine, while a book ("መጽሓፍ") is masculine. When translating thoughts, Tigrinya speakers often use "he" or "she" to refer to inanimate objects in English (e.g., calling a tractor "he" or a watch "she"). In standard English, all inanimate objects must strictly take the neuter pronoun "it" ($$\text{Inanimate Object} \rightarrow \text{it}$$), except in cases of deliberate literary personification.

cards.title: Choose subject or object pronouns
cards.problem: Correct the sentence: "Between you and I, Abel and me were the only ones who finished."

steps.text: **Step 1: After a preposition use the object form.** "between" is a preposition → between you and **me**.
**Step 2: As the subject of a verb use the subject form.** "Abel and me were" → Abel and **I** were.
**Step 3: Test by removing the other person.** "me were" is wrong; "I was/were" form is right; "between I" is wrong.
**Tip:** cover "you and" or "Abel and" and say the sentence with the pronoun alone.

cards.answer: Between you and me, Abel and I were the only ones who finished.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The scholarship committee awarded the funding to Aster and ________ after reviewing our academic portfolios.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The pronoun follows the preposition 'to' and forms part of a compound prepositional object ('to Aster and [pronoun]'). This slot requires the objective case ($$\text{Preposition} + \text{Object Pronoun}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often write 'Aster and I' because 'Aster and I' is common in the subject position. This is a typical case concord trap in matriculation exams. Applying the Cover-Up Test ('awarded the funding to me') makes the correct choice clear.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
እቲ ተውላጠ ስም ድሕሪ 'to' ዝብል መስተዋድድ (preposition) ስለ ዝመጸ፡ ኣብቲ ተቐባሊ ሓሳብ (objective case) ክስራዕ ኣለዎ። 'I' (ዋና ባእታ) ኣብዚ ቦታ ክኣቱ ኣይኽእልን እዩ። ነቲ 'Aster and' ዝብል ሓረግ ብምኽዋል 'awarded the funding to me' ኢልና ክነንብቦ ከለና ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'me' (Option B) ምዃኑ ንርዳእ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The old typewriter in the headmaster's office is still functional, but ________ keys are difficult to press.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The blank modifies the noun 'keys' to show ownership. This requires the possessive adjective 'its'.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often confuse 'its' (possessive adjective) with 'it's' (contraction of 'it is' or 'it has'). Option C ('its'') is a non-existent spelling. This spelling distinction is highly tested in national exams.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ኣብዚ ቦታ ናይ ወንነት መግለጺ ቅጽል (possessive adjective) እዩ ዘድልየና። 'Its' (ናቱ/ናታ ንዘይህይወታውያን) ዝብል ቃል ብዘይ ኮማ (apostrophe) ይጸሓፍ። 'It's' ግን ሕጽር ዝበለ ናይ 'it is' ስለ ዝኾነ ኣብዚ ቦታ ኣይሰርሕን እዩ። ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'its' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The teacher asked Ruth and ____ to collect the books.
cards.why:
**Step 1:** "Ruth and ___" is the object of "asked".

**Step 2:** Object position needs an object pronoun: me.

**Step 3:** Test: "The teacher asked me".

**Tip:** Use subject pronouns (I, he, she, we, they, who) before a verb and object pronouns (me, him, her, us, them, whom) after verbs and prepositions. Test a compound by removing the other person.

cards.title: Verbs
rule: Definition: Verbs & Auxiliary Verbs (ግሶችን ሓገዝቲ ግሶችን) refers to the syntactic system that combines lexical main verbs (which convey action, occurrence, or state of being) with primary auxiliary verbs (*be, do, have*) to express grammatical tense, aspect, mood, voice, and negation.

English verbs are fundamentally divided into lexical/main verbs (ቀንዲ ግሶች) and auxiliary/helping verbs (ሓገዝቲ ግሶች). Main verbs carry the core semantic meaning of the sentence, while auxiliary verbs are functional elements that modify the main verb to specify grammatical parameters. Lexical verbs are morphologically categorized as either regular or irregular based on how they form their past simple ($$\text{V}_2$$) and past participle ($$\text{V}_3$$) states. Regular verbs follow a predictable morphological rule of adding the suffix $$\text{Verb} + \text{-ed}$$ (e.g., *work/worked/worked*). Irregular verbs, however, do not follow this rule and undergo internal vowel mutations (e.g., *sing/sang/sung*), consonant shifts (e.g., *bend/bent/bent*), or show zero morphological change (e.g., *put/put/put*). This irregular pattern is structurally foreign to Tigrinya speakers because Tigrinya uses a non-concatenative root-and-pattern Semitic morphology (ሱር-መሰረት ግሲ) where verbs are derived from consonantal roots through highly predictable vowel templates. Consequently, English irregular verb forms must be systematically memorized for matriculation exams.

The primary auxiliary verb be (*am, is, are, was, were, been, being*) serves dual syntactic functions: it can act as a main copula verb or as a helping verb. As an auxiliary, 'be' is used to construct the continuous/progressive aspect ($$\text{be} + \text{V-ing}$$) and the passive voice ($$\text{be} + \text{V}_3$$). Tigrinya speakers often omit the 'be' auxiliary in their writing and speech (e.g., writing "She working" instead of "She is working"). This is because progressive aspect in Tigrinya can be marked morphologically directly on the main verb without requiring a separate auxiliary verb. In exams, distractors will often omit the auxiliary 'be' or present incorrect passive structures that test this exact syntactic requirement.

body: Definition: Verbs & Auxiliary Verbs (ግሶችን ሓገዝቲ ግሶችን) refers to the syntactic system that combines lexical main verbs (which convey action, occurrence, or state of being) with primary auxiliary verbs (*be, do, have*) to express grammatical tense, aspect, mood, voice, and negation.

Main verbs carry the core semantic meaning of the sentence, while auxiliary verbs are functional elements that modify the main verb to specify grammatical parameters. Lexical verbs are morphologically categorized as either regular or irregular based on how they form their past simple ($$\text{V}_2$$) and past participle ($$\text{V}_3$$) states. Irregular verbs, however, do not follow this rule and undergo internal vowel mutations (e.g., *sing/sang/sung*), consonant shifts (e.g., *bend/bent/bent*), or show zero morphological change (e.g., *put/put/put*). This irregular pattern is structurally foreign to Tigrinya speakers because Tigrinya uses a non-concatenative root-and-pattern Semitic morphology (ሱር-መሰረት ግሲ) where verbs are derived from consonantal roots through highly predictable vowel templates. Consequently, English irregular verb forms must be systematically memorized for matriculation exams.

The primary auxiliary verb be (*am, is, are, was, were, been, being*) serves dual syntactic functions: it can act as a main copula verb or as a helping verb. As an auxiliary, 'be' is used to construct the continuous/progressive aspect ($$\text{be} + \text{V-ing}$$) and the passive voice ($$\text{be} + \text{V}_3$$). Tigrinya speakers often omit the 'be' auxiliary in their writing and speech (e.g., writing "She working" instead of "She is working"). This is because progressive aspect in Tigrinya can be marked morphologically directly on the main verb without requiring a separate auxiliary verb. In exams, distractors will often omit the auxiliary 'be' or present incorrect passive structures that test this exact syntactic requirement.

The primary auxiliary verb have (*have, has, had, having*) is used to form the perfect aspect ($$\text{have/has/had} + \text{V}_3$$), representing completed actions with current relevance. Present perfect relates past events to the present, whereas past perfect ($$\text{had} + \text{V}_3$$) sequences two past events, marking the earlier action. Tigrinya lacks a direct morphological equivalent to the English Present Perfect tense. It instead relies on a gerundive form (e.g., "መጺኡ" - *he has come/he came*) or the past tense suffix. This grammatical difference makes it difficult for Tigrinya speakers to distinguish between the simple past ($$\text{V}_2$$) and the present perfect ($$\text{have/has} + \text{V}_3$$), a distinction that is a core topic in high-stakes English exams.

cards.title: Use the correct verb form after modals and auxiliaries
cards.problem: Correct the verbs: "She can sings well, and she has wrote three songs, but she don't like performing."

steps.text: **Step 1: Modal + base form.** can sings → can **sing**.
**Step 2: have/has + past participle.** has wrote → has **written**.
**Step 3: Third-person singular negative uses doesn't + base.** she don't → she **doesn't** like.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Since the local library was renovated last year, the number of visitors ________ significantly.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The subject is 'the number of visitors' (singular). The sentence describes an action that started in the past (renovated last year) and continues to have relevance in the present, requiring the present perfect tense ($$\text{has/have} + \text{V}_3$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often see 'visitors' (plural) and choose 'have increased' (Option B). However, 'The number of' is singular, requiring the singular auxiliary 'has'. Simple past 'increased' (Option C) is incorrect because the sentence links the past action to the present status.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'the number of' (ቁጽሪ ናይ...) ስለ ዝኾነ ነጸላ (singular) እዩ። ስለዚ ምስኡ ዝኸይድ ሓገዝቲ ግሲ 'has' (Option A) ክኸውን ኣለዎ። 'visitors' (ኣጋይሽ) ዝብል ቃል ብዙሕ ቁጽሪ ስለ ዝኾነ ተማሃሮ 'have' ብምምራጽ ክጋገዩ ይኽእሉ እዮም።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The science teacher asked Dawit, 'Why ________ your assignment on time yesterday?'
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
This is a direct question in the past simple tense. Questions require subject-auxiliary inversion: $$\text{Wh-word} + \text{auxiliary (didn't)} + \text{Subject (you)} + \text{base verb (complete)}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Option A incorrectly combines 'didn't' with the past tense verb 'completed'. Option B fails to invert the subject and auxiliary. In English, using 'did/didn't' requires the main verb to return to its base form, which is a highly tested rule on exams.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ሕቶ ክንሓትት ከለና እቲ ሓገዝቲ ግሲ ('didn't') ቅድሚ እቲ ዋና ባእታ ('you') ክስራዕ ኣለዎ። ከምኡ ውን 'did' ወይ 'didn't' ምስ ዝህልው፡ እቲ ቀንዲ ግሲ ወትሩ ናብቲ መበቆላዊ ቅጥዑ (base form - 'complete') ክምለስ ኣለዎ። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option C እዩ።

units.title: The English Tense System
units.intro: Grammar from Study Notes: The English Tense System: Present & Past.

cards.title: The English Tense System
rule: The English Tense System: Present & Past

Definition: The English Tense System (ናይ እንግሊዘኛ እዋን ስርዓት) is the grammatical system used to place an action or state in time (present or past) and describe its aspect—whether the action is a simple fact ($$\text{Simple Aspect}$$) or an ongoing, progressive process ($$\text{Progressive Aspect}$$).

In English, tenses do not merely express *when* an action occurs (present vs. past) but also *how* it occurs—its aspect (simple vs. progressive/continuous). Present Simple ($$\text{S} + \text{V}_{\text{1/s/es}}$$) and Present Continuous ($$\text{S} + \text{am/is/are} + \text{V-ing}$$) represent two distinct aspects of the present tense. Present Simple is used for habitual actions, general truths, and permanent states. Present Continuous is used for temporary actions happening at the exact moment of speaking. Tigrinya speakers often confuse these aspects because the boundaries between habitual actions and continuous actions are morphologically marked differently in Tigrinya. For example, the Tigrinya verb form "ይሰርሕ" can mean both "he works" (habitual) and "he is working" (continuous) depending on the helper verb "ኣሎ". This lack of a sharp morphological boundary often leads students to write "I am playing football every Saturday" instead of the correct simple present form.

examples.text: She goes to school every day.
She go to school every day.
examples.fix: She goes to school every day.

cards.title: Notes
body: The English Tense System: Present & Past

Definition: The English Tense System (ናይ እንግሊዘኛ እዋን ስርዓት) is the grammatical system used to place an action or state in time (present or past) and describe its aspect—whether the action is a simple fact ($$\text{Simple Aspect}$$) or an ongoing, progressive process ($$\text{Progressive Aspect}$$).

In English, tenses do not merely express *when* an action occurs (present vs. past) but also *how* it occurs—its aspect (simple vs. progressive/continuous). Present Simple ($$\text{S} + \text{V}_{\text{1/s/es}}$$) and Present Continuous ($$\text{S} + \text{am/is/are} + \text{V-ing}$$) represent two distinct aspects of the present tense. Present Simple is used for habitual actions, general truths, and permanent states. Present Continuous is used for temporary actions happening at the exact moment of speaking. Tigrinya speakers often confuse these aspects because the boundaries between habitual actions and continuous actions are morphologically marked differently in Tigrinya. For example, the Tigrinya verb form "ይሰርሕ" can mean both "he works" (habitual) and "he is working" (continuous) depending on the helper verb "ኣሎ". This lack of a sharp morphological boundary often leads students to write "I am playing football every Saturday" instead of the correct simple present form.

A critical area of difficulty for Tigrinya speakers is the use of Stative Verbs (ግሶች ናይ ስሚዒት ወይ ኩነታት - e.g., *know, understand, believe, want, love, seem, belong*). These verbs represent states rather than active physical processes and cannot be used in the progressive aspect ($$\times \text{I am knowing the answer}$$). Tigrinya frequently expresses states using continuous aspects (e.g., "ይርድኣኒ ኣሎ" - literally "It is understanding to me"), creating a strong L1 transfer error where students write "I am understanding the lesson" instead of "I understand the lesson." In ESSLCE exams, distractors will often present stative verbs in progressive forms to trap unwary students.

cards.title: Present perfect or past simple?
cards.problem: Complete: "I ____ (live) in Keren since 2018. Before that I ____ (live) in Mendefera for six years."

steps.text: **Step 1: Look at the time expressions.** "since 2018" links the past to now; "before that … for six years" is a finished period.
**Step 2: Unfinished period up to now → present perfect.** I have lived in Keren since 2018.
**Step 3: Finished period → past simple.** I lived in Mendefera for six years.
**Tip:** since/for + up to now → present perfect; yesterday, ago, in 2015 → past simple.

cards.answer: I have lived in Keren since 2018. Before that I lived in Mendefera for six years.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Every morning, my father ________ a cup of traditional coffee before he walks to his office.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The time-marker 'Every morning' indicates a habitual, repeated action in the present. This requires the Present Simple tense ($$\text{S} + \text{V}_{\text{1/s/es}}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often fail to match the verb to the singular subject 'my father' (3rd person singular), choosing the base form 'drink' (Option C). Option A ('is drinking') is continuous, which is incorrect for habitual actions.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Every morning' (ነፍሲ ወከፍ ንግሆ) ዝብል ናይ ግዜ መመልከቲ ልሙድ ተግባር (habitual action) ስለ ዝሕብር፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ኣብ Simple Present ክኸውን ኣለዎ። እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'my father' (ነጸላ) ስለ ዝኾነ ድማ እቲ ግሲ 's' ወሲዱ 'drinks' (Option B) ይኸውን።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Listen! The national choir ________ the anthem in the main hall right now.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The imperative 'Listen!' and 'right now' indicate an action in progress at the exact moment of speaking, requiring the Present Continuous tense ($$\text{S} + \text{am/is/are} + \text{V-ing}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students must identify 'The national choir' as a singular collective noun, which requires the singular auxiliary 'is'. Choosing 'are singing' (Option C) is a common agreement error.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Listen!' (ስምዕ!) ከምኡ ውን 'right now' (ሕጂ) ዝብሉ ቃላት እቲ ተግባር ኣብቲ ናይ ዕላል እዋን ይፍጸም ከም ዘሎ ስለ ዝሕብሩና፡ Present Continuous ክንጥቀም ኣለና። 'The national choir' (መዘምራን - ነጸላ እኩብ ስም) ስለ ዝኾነ ድማ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'is singing' (Option B) እዩ።

units.title: The English Tense System
units.intro: Grammar from Study Notes: The English Tense System: Future & Perfect Aspects.

cards.title: The English Tense System
rule: The English Tense System: Future & Perfect Aspects

Definition: The Future & Perfect Aspects (ናይ መጻኢን ፍጹም እዋናትን መልክዕ) refer to the grammatical structures used to describe completed actions connected to the present ($$\text{Present Perfect}$$), completed actions prior to a past point ($$\text{Past Perfect}$$), and various ways to express intentions, predictions, and schedules in the future.

Contrasting the Present Perfect ($$\text{Subject} + \text{have/has} + \text{V}_3$$) with the Simple Past ($$\text{Subject} + \text{V}_2$$) is a major focus of English syntax exams. Simple Past is strictly limited to actions completed at a definite, closed time in the past (e.g., *yesterday, in 2015, three days ago*). In contrast, Present Perfect describes actions that occurred at an indefinite, open time in the past, or actions that began in the past and continue to have direct relevance to the present. Tigrinya speakers often face challenges here because Tigrinya lacks a direct equivalent to the Present Perfect. Completed actions in Tigrinya are usually expressed using the gerundive verb aspect (e.g., "መጺኡ" - *he has come* or *he came*). This morphological overlap causes students to write errors like "I have seen him yesterday" because they translate the completed past state directly without applying the English rule of definite vs. indefinite time.

examples.text: She goes to school every day.
She go to school every day.
examples.fix: She goes to school every day.

cards.title: Notes
body: The English Tense System: Future & Perfect Aspects

Definition: The Future & Perfect Aspects (ናይ መጻኢን ፍጹም እዋናትን መልክዕ) refer to the grammatical structures used to describe completed actions connected to the present ($$\text{Present Perfect}$$), completed actions prior to a past point ($$\text{Past Perfect}$$), and various ways to express intentions, predictions, and schedules in the future.

Contrasting the Present Perfect ($$\text{Subject} + \text{have/has} + \text{V}_3$$) with the Simple Past ($$\text{Subject} + \text{V}_2$$) is a major focus of English syntax exams. Simple Past is strictly limited to actions completed at a definite, closed time in the past (e.g., *yesterday, in 2015, three days ago*). In contrast, Present Perfect describes actions that occurred at an indefinite, open time in the past, or actions that began in the past and continue to have direct relevance to the present. Tigrinya speakers often face challenges here because Tigrinya lacks a direct equivalent to the Present Perfect. Completed actions in Tigrinya are usually expressed using the gerundive verb aspect (e.g., "መጺኡ" - *he has come* or *he came*). This morphological overlap causes students to write errors like "I have seen him yesterday" because they translate the completed past state directly without applying the English rule of definite vs. indefinite time.

The Present Perfect relies on key time-markers (ናይ ግዜ መመልከቲታት) such as *already, yet, since, for, recently, so far, up to now, ever,* and *never*. A common exam topic is the distinction between since (which marks the exact starting point of a duration, e.g., "since 2010") and for (which marks the total length of the duration, e.g., "for ten years"). Tigrinya often uses the preposition "ካብ" (from) or time clauses in ways that blur this distinction (e.g., "ካብ 2010 ጀሚሩ" and "ንዓሰርተ ዓመት"), leading students to incorrectly write "since ten years" on exams.

cards.title: Talk about the future
cards.problem: Choose the best form: (a) "Look at those clouds! It ____ rain." (b) "I ____ meet the doctor at 10 tomorrow – it's booked." (c) "The phone is ringing." – "I ____ answer it."

steps.text: **Step 1: Prediction from present evidence → be going to.** (a) It's going to rain.
**Step 2: Fixed arrangement → present continuous.** (b) I'm meeting the doctor at 10.
**Step 3: Decision made at the moment of speaking → will.** (c) I'll answer it.
**Tip:** ask whether the future is evidence-based, arranged, or decided now.

cards.answer: (a) is going to rain; (b) am meeting; (c) will ('ll) answer.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Aster ________ in this biotechnology laboratory since she graduated from university five years ago.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The time-marker 'since she graduated' indicates an action that started in the past and continues to the present, requiring the Present Perfect Continuous tense ($$\text{S} + \text{has/have been} + \text{V-ing}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often see 'is working' (Option A) and choose it because they think of it as an ongoing present action. However, 'since' requires the perfect aspect, making 'has been working' (Option C) correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Since' (ካብቲ...) ዝብል ናይ ግዜ መመልከቲ ካብ ሕሉፍ ግዜ ጀሚሩ ክሳብ ሕጂ ዝቕጽል ተግባር ስለ ዝሕብር፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ኣብ Present Perfect Continuous ክስራዕ ኣለዎ። እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'Aster' (ነጸላ) ስለ ዝኾነ ድማ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'has been working' (Option C) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The construction company ________ the new highway road project three weeks ago.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The definite past time-marker 'three weeks ago' requires the Simple Past tense ($$\text{S} + \text{V}_2$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often confuse Present Perfect 'has completed' (Option A) with Simple Past 'completed' (Option B). Present Perfect cannot be used with definite past time-markers like 'three weeks ago'.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Three weeks ago' (ቅድሚ ሰለስተ ሰሙን) ዝብል ናይ ግዜ መመልከቲ ኣብ ሕሉፍ ግዜ ተፈጺሙ ምውድኡ ስለ ዝሕብር፡ እቲ ግሲ ብ Past Simple 'completed' (Option B) ክጸሓፍ ኣለዎ። Present Perfect ምስ 'ago' ክኸይድ ኣይኽእልን እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: My uncle is a manager in the Coca-Cola share company. He __________ there ever since he graduated from college.
cards.why: The phrase 'ever since' indicates an action that started in the past and is still continuing. Since the uncle is still a manager, the Present Perfect Continuous ('has been working') is the most appropriate.

why: This sentence describes a life experience at an indefinite past time, requiring the Present Perfect tense ($$\text{S} + \text{have/has} + \text{V}_3$$).

Speaker A: 'The phone is ringing in the living room!'

questions.label:
7. Speaker A: 'The phone is ringing in the living room!' 
Speak
why: This is a spontaneous decision made at the moment of speaking in response to an immediate situation. This requires the future auxiliary 'will' ($$\text{S} + \text{will} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$).
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.label: 8. He ________ the historic manuscript for four hours, and his
why: The durative marker 'for four hours' and the present result 'his eyes are extremely tired now' require the Present Perfect Continuous tense ($$\text{S} + \text{has/have been} + \text{V-ing}$$).

questions.q: We have lived in this historic neighborhood in Gondar ________ five years.
questions.label: 9. We have lived in this historic neighborhood in Gondar ______
why: 'Five years' is a length of duration. In English, durations of time require the preposition 'for' ($$\text{for} + \text{duration}$$).

questions.label: 15. Correct the error: "I have finished my project last week."

units.intro: Grammar from Study Notes: Question Formation & Interrogative Structures.

cards.title: Question Formation
rule: Question Formation & Interrogative Structures

Definition: Question Formation & Interrogative Structures (ሕቶኣዊ መዋቕራትን ኣሰራርዓኦምን) refers to the syntactic rules governing the creation of direct and indirect questions, including yes/no questions, Wh-questions, subject vs. object questions, and embedded clauses, utilizing auxiliary inversion and precise word order.

English interrogative structures are fundamentally divided into direct questions ($$\text{Direct Questions}$$) and indirect or embedded questions ($$\text{Indirect Questions}$$). To signal a direct question, English strictly requires grammatical inversion, where the auxiliary verb is placed before the subject ($$\text{Auxiliary} + \text{Subject} + \text{Verb}$$), or the introduction of a dummy auxiliary. Tigrinya, conversely, forms yes/no questions synthetically by attaching the suffix particle "-ዶ" (do) directly to the inflected main verb (e.g., "መጺኡ" [he came] $$\rightarrow$$ "መጺኡዶ?" [did he come?]). It does not employ auxiliary inversion. Wh-questions in Tigrinya insert the question word directly into the standard declarative Subject-Object-Verb slot without modifying the word order (e.g., "ንስኻ ኣበይ ትነብር?" [Where do you live?]). Because Tigrinya lacks auxiliary inversion and dummy 'do'-support, students frequently make word order errors in direct English questions (e.g., writing "Where you are going?" instead of "Where *are you* going?").

examples.text: She goes to school every day.
She go to school every day.
examples.fix: She goes to school every day.

cards.title: Notes
body: Question Formation & Interrogative Structures

Definition: Question Formation & Interrogative Structures (ሕቶኣዊ መዋቕራትን ኣሰራርዓኦምን) refers to the syntactic rules governing the creation of direct and indirect questions, including yes/no questions, Wh-questions, subject vs. object questions, and embedded clauses, utilizing auxiliary inversion and precise word order.

English interrogative structures are fundamentally divided into direct questions ($$\text{Direct Questions}$$) and indirect or embedded questions ($$\text{Indirect Questions}$$). To signal a direct question, English strictly requires grammatical inversion, where the auxiliary verb is placed before the subject ($$\text{Auxiliary} + \text{Subject} + \text{Verb}$$), or the introduction of a dummy auxiliary. Tigrinya, conversely, forms yes/no questions synthetically by attaching the suffix particle "-ዶ" (do) directly to the inflected main verb (e.g., "መጺኡ" [he came] $$\rightarrow$$ "መጺኡዶ?" [did he come?]). It does not employ auxiliary inversion. Wh-questions in Tigrinya insert the question word directly into the standard declarative Subject-Object-Verb slot without modifying the word order (e.g., "ንስኻ ኣበይ ትነብር?" [Where do you live?]). Because Tigrinya lacks auxiliary inversion and dummy 'do'-support, students frequently make word order errors in direct English questions (e.g., writing "Where you are going?" instead of "Where *are you* going?").

Direct Yes/No questions require the syntactic pattern $$\text{Auxiliary} + \text{Subject} + \text{Verb} \dots ?$$. In the simple present and simple past tenses, where no auxiliary is naturally present in active declarative clauses, English inserts the dummy auxiliary "do" ($$\text{Do/Does/Did} + \text{Subject} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$). A common error on national exams is failing to return the main verb to its base form after using "do/does/did" (e.g., writing "Did she *went*?" instead of the correct "Did she *go*?"). Tigrinya speakers must remember that the tense marker is carried entirely by the auxiliary, leaving the main verb in its bare infinitive state.

cards.title: Form wh-questions about the subject and the object
cards.problem: Ask questions about the underlined words in "Samuel helped Ruth." (a) about Samuel, (b) about Ruth.

steps.text: **Step 1: Subject question – the wh-word replaces the subject, no auxiliary.** (a) Who helped Ruth?
**Step 2: Object question – wh-word + auxiliary + subject + base verb.** (b) Who(m) did Samuel help?
**Step 3: Check the verb form.** In (b) "did" carries the past, so the verb is base "help".
**Tip:** if the answer is the subject, do not add do/does/did.

cards.answer: (a) Who helped Ruth? (b) Who(m) did Samuel help?

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Could you please tell me what time ________ from the regional airport tomorrow morning?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
This is an indirect (embedded) question introduced by the polite phrase 'Could you please tell me'. It requires declarative word order: $$\text{Wh-word (what time)} + \text{Subject (the flight)} + \text{Verb (departs)}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose Option A ('does the flight depart') or Option C ('will the flight depart') because they assume they need direct question inversion. However, indirect questions must not use auxiliary inversion or dummy do-support.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
እዚ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ብ 'Could you please...' ዝጅምር ውሽጣዊ ሕቶ (Indirect/Embedded question) እዩ። ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ውሽጣዊ ሕቶታት ስርዓተ-ሕቶ (inversion) ኣይህልዎምን፤ ልክዕ ከም ስሩዕ ኣዎንታዊ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ($$Subject + Verb$$) እዮም ዝጸሓፉ። ስለዚ እቲ ዋና ባእታ 'the flight' ቅድሚ እቲ ግሲ 'departs' ክስራዕ ኣለዎ (Option B)። 'does the flight depart' ምጥቃም ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why ________ your science project on time last Friday, as the teacher requested?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
This is a direct past Wh-question. It requires the past dummy auxiliary 'didn't' to precede the subject 'you', and the main verb must return to its base form: $$\text{Why} + \text{didn't} + \text{Subject} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Option A incorrectly combines 'didn't' with the past tense verb 'submitted'. Option B fails to invert the subject and auxiliary. Option C correctly uses 'didn't' with the base verb 'submit'.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ቀጥታዊ ሕሉፍ ሕቶ ክንሓትት ከለና እቲ ሓገዝቲ ግሲ ('didn't') ቅድሚ እቲ ዋና ባእታ ('you') ክስራዕ ኣለዎ። ከምኡ ውን 'did' ወይ 'didn't' ምስ ዝህልው፡ እቲ ቀንዲ ግሲ ወትሩ ናብቲ መበቆላዊ ቅጥዑ (base form - 'submit') ክምለስ ኣለዎ። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option C እዩ።

units.title: Question Tags
units.intro: Grammar from Study Notes: Question Tags & Short Additions.

cards.title: Question Tags
rule: Definition: Question Tags & Short Additions (ሕቶኣዊ ጭራታትን ሓጸርቲ መወሰኽታታትን) are syntactic structures used to seek confirmation at the end of a statement (question tags) or to express agreement or disagreement with a previous statement (short additions) using auxiliary matching and subject-verb inversion.

Question tags (ሕቶኣዊ ጭራታት) are short clauses appended to declarative or imperative sentences to transform them into questions. The foundational rule of tag formation is polarity opposition: a positive statement requires a negative tag ($$\text{Positive Statement} \rightarrow \text{Negative Tag}$$), and a negative statement requires a positive tag ($$\text{Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$). Tigrinya possesses no direct equivalent to this matching system; instead, it utilizes invariant terminal expressions such as "ኣይኮነን?" (isn't it?) or the question particle "-ዶ" regardless of the subject, verb, or polarity of the preceding clause (e.g., "ንሱ መምህር እዩ፡ ኣይኮነን?" and "ንሳቶም ከይዶም እዮም፡ ኣይኮነን?"). This lack of structural variation in L1 causes Tigrinya-speaking students to overgeneralize and write "isn't it?" or "no?" at the end of all English statements, making tag formation a heavily tested diagnostic area on national exams.

To construct a grammatically correct question tag, the auxiliary verb of the tag must match the auxiliary verb of the main clause in tense, aspect, and number. If the main clause does not contain an auxiliary verb (as in active simple present or simple past clauses), the tag must introduce dummy do-support ($$\text{Simple Present} \rightarrow \text{don't/doesn't}$$ and $$\text{Simple Past} \rightarrow \text{didn't}$$ — e.g. "She works here, *doesn't she*?", "They left early, *didn't they*?").

examples.text: She goes to school every day.
She go to school every day.
examples.fix: She goes to school every day.

cards.title: Notes
body: Definition: Question Tags & Short Additions (ሕቶኣዊ ጭራታትን ሓጸርቲ መወሰኽታታትን) are syntactic structures used to seek confirmation at the end of a statement (question tags) or to express agreement or disagreement with a previous statement (short additions) using auxiliary matching and subject-verb inversion.

Question tags (ሕቶኣዊ ጭራታት) are short clauses appended to declarative or imperative sentences to transform them into questions. The foundational rule of tag formation is polarity opposition: a positive statement requires a negative tag ($$\text{Positive Statement} \rightarrow \text{Negative Tag}$$), and a negative statement requires a positive tag ($$\text{Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$). Tigrinya possesses no direct equivalent to this matching system; instead, it utilizes invariant terminal expressions such as "ኣይኮነን?" (isn't it?) or the question particle "-ዶ" regardless of the subject, verb, or polarity of the preceding clause (e.g., "ንሱ መምህር እዩ፡ ኣይኮነን?" and "ንሳቶም ከይዶም እዮም፡ ኣይኮነን?"). This lack of structural variation in L1 causes Tigrinya-speaking students to overgeneralize and write "isn't it?" or "no?" at the end of all English statements, making tag formation a heavily tested diagnostic area on national exams.

To construct a grammatically correct question tag, the auxiliary verb of the tag must match the auxiliary verb of the main clause in tense, aspect, and number. If the main clause does not contain an auxiliary verb (as in active simple present or simple past clauses), the tag must introduce dummy do-support ($$\text{Simple Present} \rightarrow \text{don't/doesn't}$$ and $$\text{Simple Past} \rightarrow \text{didn't}$$ — e.g. "She works here, *doesn't she*?", "They left early, *didn't they*?").

Several irregular patterns and syntactic exceptions are common filters on the matriculation exam. The first-person singular copula "I am" requires the irregular negative tag aren't I? (e.g., "I am late, *aren't I*?"). However, the negative statement "I am not" follows the regular pattern, taking "am I?" (e.g., "I am not late, *am I*?"). Suggestions starting with "Let's" require the tag shall we? (e.g., "Let's take a break, *shall we*?"). Imperatives usually take *will you?* or *won't you?* (e.g., "Close the door, *will you*?"), and statements with negative words such as *never, hardly, nobody* take a positive tag (e.g., "He never comes late, *does he*?").

cards.title: Add the correct question tag
cards.problem: Add tags: (a) "You're coming, ___?" (b) "She didn't call, ___?" (c) "Let's go, ___?" (d) "Nobody saw it, ___?"

steps.text: **Step 1: Positive statement → negative tag; negative → positive.**
**Step 2: Repeat the auxiliary and use a pronoun.** (a) aren't you? (b) did she?
**Step 3: Special cases.** "Let's" → shall we? (c). Nobody/no one is negative in meaning and takes "they" → (d) did they?
**Tip:** words like never, nobody and hardly make the statement negative, so the tag is positive.

cards.answer: (a) aren't you? (b) did she? (c) shall we? (d) did they?

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I am late for the registration of the national matriculation examination, ________?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The main clause starts with the positive first-person singular copula 'I am'. This requires an irregular negative question tag in standard English: $$\text{I am} \rightarrow \text{aren't I?}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'am not I' (Option A) because they try to follow regular polarity rules, or 'isn't it' (Option D) due to L1 transfer. Option B 'aren't I' is the correct irregular grammatical exception.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ወግዓዊ ሰዋስው፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ብ 'I am' (ኣነ...) ምስ ዝጅምር፡ እቲ ናቱ ፍሉይ ሕቶኣዊ ጭራ (question tag) ወትሩ 'aren't I?' (Option B - ኣይኮንኩን?) እዩ ዝኸውን። 'am not I' ምጥቃም ዓቢ ጌጋ እዩ ምኽንያቱ ከምዚ ዝበለ መዋቕር ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ሰዋስው ስለ ዘየለ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She rarely visits her relatives in Gondar during the long academic vacations, ________?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The adverb 'rarely' is semi-negative, which makes the main statement grammatically negative. This requires a positive question tag with present simple dummy do-support ($$\text{Semi-Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often see the positive verb spelling 'visits' and automatically select a negative tag like 'doesn't she' (Option A). However, because 'rarely' is negative, the positive tag 'does she' (Option B) is correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Rarely' (ሳሕቲ/ኣዝዩ ውሑድ ግዜ) ዝብል ቃል ኣሉታዊ ቃና (semi-negative) ስለ ዘለዎ፡ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ከም ኣሉታዊ ይውሰድ። ስለዚ እቲ ዝስዕብ ሕቶኣዊ ጭራ ብኣዎንታዊ ሓገዝቲ ግሲ 'does she' (Option B) ክኸውን ኣለዎ። 'doesn't she' ምምራጽ ናይዚ ሕጊ መጻወድያ እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: She rarely ever goes to cinema_______?
cards.why: The word 'rarely' is semi-negative, which makes the whole sentence negative. Negative sentences require positive question tags. Since the verb is 'goes' (Present Simple), the tag is 'does she'.

games.title: Match the statement to its tag

questions.q: I am late for the registration of the national matriculation examination, ________?
questions.label: 1. I am late for the registration of the national matriculation
why: The main clause starts with the positive first-person singular copula 'I am'. This requires an irregular negative question tag in standard English: $$\text{I am} \rightarrow \text{aren't I?}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: She rarely visits her relatives in Gondar during the long academic vacations, ________?
questions.label: 2. She rarely visits her relatives in Gondar during the long ac
why: The adverb 'rarely' is semi-negative, which makes the main statement grammatically negative. This requires a positive question tag with present simple dummy do-support ($$\text{Semi-Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$).
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Everyone was extremely excited about the university scholarship announcement, ________?
questions.label: 3. Everyone was extremely excited about the university scholars
why: Indefinite pronouns referring to people ('everyone') require the plural pronoun 'they' in the tag. Because the pronoun is plural, the past copula 'was' must shift to plural 'weren't' to maintain agreement.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Let's take a brief walk in the school garden before the final lecture begins, ________?
questions.label: 4. Let's take a brief walk in the school garden before the fina
why: Suggestions starting with 'Let's' (contraction of 'Let us') require the irregular question tag 'shall we?' in standard English.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: She doesn't speak French fluently, ________?
questions.label: 5. She doesn't speak French fluently, ________?
why: The main clause is negative ('doesn't speak'). This requires a positive question tag using the matching auxiliary 'does': $$\text{Negative Statement} \rightarrow \text{Positive Tag}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q:
Speaker A: 'I really love studying English literature.' 
Speaker B: '________'
questions.label:
6. Speaker A: 'I really love studying English literature.' 
Spe
why: Speaker A's statement is positive and in the Simple Present tense (no auxiliary present). Speaker B wants to show agreement, requiring the inverted positive agreement structure: $$\text{So} + \text{do/does} + \text{Subject}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q:
Speaker A: 'I don't like drinking hot tea in the afternoon.' 
Speaker B: '________'
questions.label: 7. Speaker A: 'I don't like drinking hot tea in the afternoon.'
why: Speaker A's statement is negative ('don't like'). To show agreement with a negative statement, Speaker B must use the inverted negative agreement structure: $$\text{Neither/Nor} + \text{Auxiliary} + \text{Subject}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Nothing went wrong during the school laboratory experiment, ________?
questions.label: 8. Nothing went wrong during the school laboratory experiment,
why: The subject 'Nothing' is negative, which makes the main statement grammatically negative. This requires a positive question tag with past simple dummy do-support and the singular pronoun 'it'.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Don't make any noise while the national exam is in progress, ________?
questions.label: 9. Don't make any noise while the national exam is in progress,
why: Negative imperatives (commands starting with 'Don't') strictly require the positive tag 'will you?' in standard English.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: The university dean has already signed the official graduation list, ________?
questions.label: 10. The university dean has already signed the official graduati
why: The main clause contains the positive perfect auxiliary 'has' ('has already signed'). This requires a negative question tag with the matching auxiliary 'hasn't' and pronoun 'he': $$\text{Positive Statement} \rightarrow \text{Negative Tag}$$.
questions.tip: Read the whole sentence before choosing.

questions.q: Punctuation marks are very important in writing, _______?
why:
To form a question tag:
1. Use the auxiliary verb from the statement ('are').
2. If the statement is positive, the tag must be negative ('aren't').
3. Use the pronoun that corresponds to the subject ('Punctuation marks' = 'they').
Result: **'aren't they'**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: None of the students is trying, ___________?
why: The word 'None' makes the sentence negative, so the question tag must be positive. Since 'students' is plural, the pronoun 'they' is used. Therefore, 'Are they' is the correct tag.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Selam: I hope it is going to be a minor surgery, **61**?
why: **Rule:** A question tag uses the auxiliary verb from the main sentence. Since the main sentence is positive ('it **is** going to be'), the tag must be negative: **'isn't it?'**.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Only two students understood the instruction, ___?
why: The main sentence is positive and in the Simple Past ('understood'). Therefore, the question tag must be negative and use the auxiliary 'did' ('didn't they').
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Suleman: This coat looks nice for such a chilly weather, __________?
why: **Rule:** For a positive statement in Present Simple ("This coat looks"), the tag must be negative using the auxiliary 'do/does'. Since "coat" is singular, we use "doesn't it".
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Open the door_______?
why: For imperative sentences (commands or requests), 'will you' is the most common and standard question tag used to invite cooperation.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Don't open the question paper until you are told to do so, _____________?
why: For negative imperatives (commands starting with 'Don't'), the standard question tag is 'will you'.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: All the teachers are working hard this semester, (38) ______.
why: To add a positive statement that agree with a previous positive statement, we use 'so + auxiliary verb + subject'. Since the first clause uses 'are', the addition is 'so are the students'.
questions.tip: Read every option before choosing; rule out the ones that contradict the notes.

questions.q: Nobody phoned while I was out, ____?
questions.label: 19. Nobody phoned while I was out, ____?

similar.q: Tag: Everyone enjoyed the party, ____?
Tag: Nothing happened, ____?

why: "Nobody" makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive.
Indefinite pronouns like nobody/everyone take "they" in the tag.
questions.tip: Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag. Use the same auxiliary (or do/does/did). Special: I am → aren't I; Let's → shall we.

questions.q: You'd better leave now, ____?
questions.label: 20. You'd better leave now, ____?

similar.q: Tag: You'd rather stay, ____?
Tag: She'd finished, ____?

why: The auxiliary is "had", so the tag uses "hadn't".
So: You'd better leave now, hadn't you?
questions.tip: Positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag. Use the same auxiliary (or do/does/did). Special: I am → aren't I; Let's → shall we.

rule: Word Formation, Affixes & Derivational Morphology

Definition: Word Formation and Derivational Morphology (ስነ-ቅርጺ ቃላትን ምምስራት ሓደሽቲ ቃላትን) refers to the processes of creating new words from existing root words by adding prefixes and suffixes, thereby modifying their semantic meaning or converting them into different grammatical word classes.

English word formation is heavily dependent on concatenative morphology, where prefixes (added to the beginning of a root) and suffixes (added to the end of a root) are sequentially attached to a base form ($$\text{Prefix} + \text{Root} + \text{Suffix}$$). In contrast, Tigrinya uses a Semitic root-and-pattern (consonantal root) system. In Tigrinya, word class conversion and nominalization are primarily achieved through internal vowel melody shifts and consonant doubling within a triconsonantal root (e.g., the root {s-b-r} meaning 'to break' produces "ስባር" [broken piece] or "ስባረ" [fracture]) rather than the linear affixation typical of English. This fundamental morphological difference is a major conceptual hurdle for Tigrinya-speaking students, who must transition from an internal consonantal modification system to a linear, suffix-based word-building system.

examples.text: She goes to school every day.
She go to school every day.
examples.fix: She goes to school every day.

cards.title: Notes
body: Word Formation, Affixes & Derivational Morphology

Definition: Word Formation and Derivational Morphology (ስነ-ቅርጺ ቃላትን ምምስራት ሓደሽቲ ቃላትን) refers to the processes of creating new words from existing root words by adding prefixes and suffixes, thereby modifying their semantic meaning or converting them into different grammatical word classes.

English word formation is heavily dependent on concatenative morphology, where prefixes (added to the beginning of a root) and suffixes (added to the end of a root) are sequentially attached to a base form ($$\text{Prefix} + \text{Root} + \text{Suffix}$$). In contrast, Tigrinya uses a Semitic root-and-pattern (consonantal root) system. In Tigrinya, word class conversion and nominalization are primarily achieved through internal vowel melody shifts and consonant doubling within a triconsonantal root (e.g., the root {s-b-r} meaning 'to break' produces "ስባር" [broken piece] or "ስባረ" [fracture]) rather than the linear affixation typical of English. This fundamental morphological difference is a major conceptual hurdle for Tigrinya-speaking students, who must transition from an internal consonantal modification system to a linear, suffix-based word-building system.

Nominalization (ምስራሕ ስማት) is the process of converting verbs or adjectives into nouns. Verbs are converted to nouns using suffixes like *-ment, -tion, -sion, -ance, -ence, -al* ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Suffix} \rightarrow \text{Noun}$$, e.g., *agree* $$\rightarrow$$ *agreement*, *decide* $$\rightarrow$$ *decision*, *assist* $$\rightarrow$$ *assistance*). Adjectives are converted to nouns using suffixes like *-ness, -ity, -dom, -hood, -ship* ($$\text{Adjective} + \text{Suffix} \rightarrow \text{Noun}$$, e.g., *happy* $$\rightarrow$$ *happiness*, *pure* $$\rightarrow$$ *purity*, *free* $$\rightarrow$$ *freedom*). National examinations frequently test these nominalized forms in subject and object slots, requiring students to identify spelling adjustments (e.g., dropping 'y' to 'i' in *happiness* or consonant shifts in *decide* $$\rightarrow$$ *decision*).

cards.title: Build words with affixes
cards.problem: Complete with a form of the word in brackets: "The plan was ____ (success) because the team was ____ (organise) and ____ (honest) was rewarded."

steps.text: **Step 1: Find the needed word class.** After "was" and before "because" → adjective; after "was" describing the team → adjective (participle); subject of a verb → noun.
**Step 2: Add the suffix.** success + -ful → successful; organise + -ed → organised; honest + -y → honesty.
**Step 3: Check the meaning and spelling.**
**Tip:** -ful/-ous/-ive make adjectives; -ness/-ity/-ment/-y make nouns; un-/dis-/in- change the meaning, not the class.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The sudden ________ of the school principal surprised both the teachers and the students.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The blank follows the article 'The' and the adjective 'sudden', requiring a noun ($$\text{Article} + \text{Adjective} + \text{Noun}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose the verb 'depart' (Option A) due to direct translation. Only the nominalized form 'departure' (Option B), formed by adding the suffix '-ure' to the verb 'depart', is grammatically correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
እቲ ባዶ ቦታ ድሕሪ 'The' (ኣንቀጽ) ከምኡ ውን ድሕሪ 'sudden' (ቅጽል) ስለ ዝመጸ፡ ብግድን ስም (noun) ክኸውን ኣለዎ። እቲ 'depart' (ምኻድ) ዝብል ግሲ ናብ ስም ክቕየር ከሎ ድማ 'departure' (Option B - ምኻድ/ምስጓም) ይኸውን። 'depart' ምጥቃም ሰዋስዋዊ ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The instructions provided by the examiner were highly ________, which caused many candidates to make mistakes.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The context 'which caused many candidates to make mistakes' indicates a negative adjective is required to describe the instructions.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often struggle with negative prefixes and choose 'disclear' (Option C) or 'inclear' (Option D). The correct negative prefix for the adjective 'clear' is 'un-', forming 'unclear' (Option B).

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ተመሃሮ ጌጋ ከም ዝገበሩ ስለ ዝገለጸ፡ እቲ መግለጺ 'ዘይነጸረ' (negative adjective) ክኸውን ኣለዎ። ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ን 'clear' (ንጹር) ኣሉታዊ ክንገብሮ ከለና እንጥቅመሉ ቅድመ-መጣበቕታ 'un-' ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'unclear' (Option B - ዘይንጹር) እዩ።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the correct form: "Her ____ to help others is admirable."
cards.why:
**Step 1:** After "Her" (a possessive) we need a noun.

**Step 2:** willing + -ness → willingness.

**Step 3:** "willing" is an adjective and "willingly" an adverb.

**Tip:** Look at the position: after an article → noun; before a noun → adjective; describing a verb → adverb; after "to" or a subject → verb. Then add the suffix that makes that part of speech.

units.title: Phrasal Verbs
units.intro: Grammar from Study Notes ch.16: Phrasal Verbs & Prepositional Verbs.

cards.title: Phrasal Verbs
rule: Definition: Phrasal and Prepositional Verbs (ቅጽል ግሶችን መስተዋድዳዊ ግሶችን) are multi-word verb combinations consisting of a lexical verb paired with an adverbial particle (*phrasal verb*) or a grammatical preposition (*prepositional verb*), resulting in a unified vocabulary unit with a distinct, often highly idiomatic meaning.

Phrasal verbs consist of a main verb and an adverbial particle (e.g., *up, off, out, down, on*). Prepositional verbs, by contrast, consist of a main verb followed strictly by a grammatical preposition (e.g., *look at, cope with, rely on*). The core linguistic challenge is that phrasal verbs are highly idiomatic: their combined meaning is completely different from the literal meanings of the individual words (e.g., *give* [ምሃብ] vs. *give up* [ተስፋ ምቝራጽ/ምሕዳግ]). Since Tigrinya lacks phrasal verbs and relies on single, highly inflected lexical verbs (e.g., "ተስፋ ቆረጸ" for *give up*, "ኣቋረጸ" for *call off*), students must memorize these multi-word combinations as distinct vocabulary items to succeed on national examinations.

Syntactic separability (ስውር ሰዋስው ናይ ምፍልላይ) is a major exam focus for transitive phrasal verbs. If a phrasal verb is separable, a noun object can sit either after the particle or between the verb and the particle ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Particle} + \text{Noun Object}$$ or $$\text{Verb} + \text{Noun Object} + \text{Particle}$$, e.g., "write down the formula" or "write the formula down"). However, if the object is a pronoun (እቲ ተቐባሊ ተውላጠ ስም እንተኾይኑ), it **must** strictly be placed between the verb and the particle ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Pronoun Object} + \text{Particle}$$, e.g., "write *it* down"). Writing $$\times \text{write down it}$$ is a major syntactic error on matriculation exams. Tigrinya speakers often make this error because they naturally want to keep the verbal unit together, reflecting their L1 pronominal suffix habits.

cards.title: Notes
body: Definition: Phrasal and Prepositional Verbs (ቅጽል ግሶችን መስተዋድዳዊ ግሶችን) are multi-word verb combinations consisting of a lexical verb paired with an adverbial particle (*phrasal verb*) or a grammatical preposition (*prepositional verb*), resulting in a unified vocabulary unit with a distinct, often highly idiomatic meaning.

Phrasal verbs consist of a main verb and an adverbial particle (e.g., *up, off, out, down, on*). Prepositional verbs, by contrast, consist of a main verb followed strictly by a grammatical preposition (e.g., *look at, cope with, rely on*). The core linguistic challenge is that phrasal verbs are highly idiomatic: their combined meaning is completely different from the literal meanings of the individual words (e.g., *give* [ምሃብ] vs. *give up* [ተስፋ ምቝራጽ/ምሕዳግ]). Since Tigrinya lacks phrasal verbs and relies on single, highly inflected lexical verbs (e.g., "ተስፋ ቆረጸ" for *give up*, "ኣቋረጸ" for *call off*), students must memorize these multi-word combinations as distinct vocabulary items to succeed on national examinations.

Syntactic separability (ስውር ሰዋስው ናይ ምፍልላይ) is a major exam focus for transitive phrasal verbs. If a phrasal verb is separable, a noun object can sit either after the particle or between the verb and the particle ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Particle} + \text{Noun Object}$$ or $$\text{Verb} + \text{Noun Object} + \text{Particle}$$, e.g., "write down the formula" or "write the formula down"). However, if the object is a pronoun (እቲ ተቐባሊ ተውላጠ ስም እንተኾይኑ), it **must** strictly be placed between the verb and the particle ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Pronoun Object} + \text{Particle}$$, e.g., "write *it* down"). Writing $$\times \text{write down it}$$ is a major syntactic error on matriculation exams. Tigrinya speakers often make this error because they naturally want to keep the verbal unit together, reflecting their L1 pronominal suffix habits.

Inseparable phrasal and prepositional verbs do not allow any separation under any circumstances. Regardless of whether the object is a noun or a pronoun, it must strictly follow the particle or preposition ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Preposition/Particle} + \text{Object}$$, e.g., "look after the children" or "look after *them*"). Writing $$\times \text{look them after}$$ is grammatically incorrect. Common inseparable combinations tested on the ESSLCE include *run into* (to meet by chance), *cope with* (to handle), *rely on* (to trust), and *look after* (to take care of).

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Because of the heavy rainfall and flooding, the school principal had to ________ the sports competition.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The context 'heavy rainfall and flooding' indicates that the sports competition had to be canceled.
We need a phrasal verb meaning to cancel.
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Because of the heavy rainfall and flooding, the school principal had to ________ the sports competition.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The context 'heavy rainfall and flooding' indicates that the sports competition had to be canceled. We need a phrasal verb meaning to cancel.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often confuse 'put off' (to postpone) with 'call off' (to cancel). While both are common, 'call off' (Option B) is the correct phrasal verb meaning to cancel an event.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Call off' (ምስራዝ) ዝብል ቅጽል ግሲ ንሓደ መደብ ወይ ውድድር ምሉእ ብምሉእ ንምስራዝ የገልግል። 'Put off' (ምስጋጋር) ግን ሓደ መደብ ንኻልእ ግዜ ምስጋጋር ንምግላጽ እዩ። ኣብዚ ብሰንኪ ውሕጅን ከቢድ ዝናብን እቲ ውድድር ስለ ዝተሰረዘ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'call off' (Option B) እዩ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: I have finished reading this reference book; please ________ to the library assistant.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
'Hand in' (to submit/return) is a transitive separable phrasal verb.
Since the object is the pronoun 'it', it must strictly be placed between the verb and the particle ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Pronoun} + \text{Particle}$$).
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: I have finished reading this reference book; please ________ to the library assistant.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
'Hand in' (to submit/return) is a transitive separable phrasal verb. Since the object is the pronoun 'it', it must strictly be placed between the verb and the particle ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Pronoun} + \text{Particle}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Option B 'hand in it' places the pronoun at the end, which violates the pronoun separation rule. Option D 'hand it down' has an incorrect meaning (to pass to next generation). Option C is correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Hand in' (ምምላስ/ምርካብ) ዝብል ቃል ዝፈላለ (separable) ቅጽል ግሲ እዩ። እቲ ተቐባሊ ሓሳብ 'it' (ተውላጠ ስም) ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ብግድን ኣብ ማእከል እቲ ግሲን እታ መጣበቕታን ክስራዕ ኣለዎ ('hand it in' - Option C)። 'hand in it' ምጥቃም ዓቢ ናይ ሰዋስው ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: The high school laboratory has ________ chemical solutions, so the practical test has been postponed.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The context 'so the practical test has been postponed' indicates that the laboratory has exhausted its supply of chemical solutions.
We need a phrasal verb meaning to exhaust a supply.
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The high school laboratory has ________ chemical solutions, so the practical test has been postponed.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The context 'so the practical test has been postponed' indicates that the laboratory has exhausted its supply of chemical solutions. We need a phrasal verb meaning to exhaust a supply.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students must identify 'run out of' (Option A) as the correct three-word phrasal verb meaning to exhaust. 'Run into' means to meet by chance, and 'put up with' means to tolerate.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Run out of' (ምውዳእ/ምሕላቕ) ዝብል ሰለስተ ቃላት ዘለዎ ቅጽል ግሲ፡ ዘለካ ቀረብ ወይ ቀዋሚ ነገር ምሉእ ብምሉእ ክውዳእ ከሎ ንምግላጽ የገልግል። ኣብዚ እቲ ኬሚካል ስለ ዝተወድአ ቅኑዕ መልሲ 'run out of' (Option A) እዩ።

cards.title: Fixed Prepositional Patterns
rule: Definition: Fixed Prepositional Patterns (ቋሚ መስተዋድዳዊ ቅርጽታት) are abstract syntactic collocations where specific verbs, adjectives, or nouns must strictly be paired with designated prepositions. These combinations are idiomatic and cannot be determined through literal translation.

In English, prepositions are not always used to express literal relationships of space or time. Instead, they often function as bound lexical partners to specific words ($$\text{Word} + \text{Preposition}$$). Unlike English, Tigrinya utilizes a small, generalized set of clitic prepositions prefixed directly to nouns (e.g., "ብ-" [by/with/for], "ን-" [to/for], "ኣብ" [in/on/at], "ናብ" [to/towards]). Because a single Tigrinya prefix corresponds to multiple English prepositions, Tigrinya speakers consistently experience negative language transfer (ኣሉታዊ ምስግጋር ቋንቋ) when attempting to translate prepositions literally. This systematic grammatical divergence is heavily exploited by exam writers in high-stakes national examinations.

Adjective-preposition collocations represent a highly tested category. Key patterns include *interested in* ($$\text{Adjective} + \text{in}$$), *good/bad/clever at* ($$\text{Adjective} + \text{at}$$), *afraid of* ($$\text{Adjective} + \text{of}$$), and *proud of* ($$\text{Adjective} + \text{of}$$). A classic matriculation trap arises with the adjective *good* when describing skill or proficiency. In Tigrinya, one uses the locative prefix "ኣብ" (in/at), saying "ንሱ ኣብ ሒሳብ ጎበዝ እዩ" (literally: in mathematics he is skilled). Direct L1 transfer leads students to write or select the incorrect English forms $$\times \text{good in mathematics}$$ or $$\times \text{clever in English}$$. In standard English, the only correct collocation is *good at* ($$\text{good} + \text{at} + \text{Noun/Gerund}$$).

body: Definition: Fixed Prepositional Patterns (ቋሚ መስተዋድዳዊ ቅርጽታት) are abstract syntactic collocations where specific verbs, adjectives, or nouns must strictly be paired with designated prepositions. These combinations are idiomatic and cannot be determined through literal translation.

In English, prepositions are not always used to express literal relationships of space or time. Instead, they often function as bound lexical partners to specific words ($$\text{Word} + \text{Preposition}$$). Unlike English, Tigrinya utilizes a small, generalized set of clitic prepositions prefixed directly to nouns (e.g., "ብ-" [by/with/for], "ን-" [to/for], "ኣብ" [in/on/at], "ናብ" [to/towards]). Because a single Tigrinya prefix corresponds to multiple English prepositions, Tigrinya speakers consistently experience negative language transfer (ኣሉታዊ ምስግጋር ቋንቋ) when attempting to translate prepositions literally. This systematic grammatical divergence is heavily exploited by exam writers in high-stakes national examinations.

Adjective-preposition collocations represent a highly tested category. Key patterns include *interested in* ($$\text{Adjective} + \text{in}$$), *good/bad/clever at* ($$\text{Adjective} + \text{at}$$), *afraid of* ($$\text{Adjective} + \text{of}$$), and *proud of* ($$\text{Adjective} + \text{of}$$). A classic matriculation trap arises with the adjective *good* when describing skill or proficiency. In Tigrinya, one uses the locative prefix "ኣብ" (in/at), saying "ንሱ ኣብ ሒሳብ ጎበዝ እዩ" (literally: in mathematics he is skilled). Direct L1 transfer leads students to write or select the incorrect English forms $$\times \text{good in mathematics}$$ or $$\times \text{clever in English}$$. In standard English, the only correct collocation is *good at* ($$\text{good} + \text{at} + \text{Noun/Gerund}$$).

Verb-preposition patterns also contain significant transfer traps. Key collocations include *congratulate on* ($$\text{Verb} + \text{on}$$), *accuse of* ($$\text{Verb} + \text{of}$$), *depend on* ($$\text{Verb} + \text{on}$$), and *suffer from* ($$\text{Verb} + \text{from}$$). Tigrinya speakers routinely write the incorrect $$\times \text{congratulate you for passing}$$ because they translate "ብምሓለፍካ" (for/by your passing) as "for". The correct English pattern is strictly *congratulate someone on something* ($$\text{congratulate} + \text{Object} + \text{on} + \text{Noun/Gerund}$$). Similarly, *accuse* must be paired with *of* (e.g., *accuse of theft*), whereas translating literally from Tigrinya "ብምስራቕ ተኸሲሱ" often results in the incorrect use of *with* or *by*.

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: The school principal warmly congratulated the top-performing students ________ achieving straight A's on the ESSLCE.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The verb 'congratulate' requires the preposition 'on' followed by a noun or gerund: $$\text{congratulate} + \text{someone} + \text{on} + \text{something}$$.
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'for' (Option A) because they translate 'ብምሓለፍካ' (for your passing) directly into English.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The school principal warmly congratulated the top-performing students ________ achieving straight A's on the ESSLCE.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The verb 'congratulate' requires the preposition 'on' followed by a noun or gerund: $$\text{congratulate} + \text{someone} + \text{on} + \text{something}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'for' (Option A) because they translate 'ብምሓለፍካ' (for your passing) directly into English. This is a classic negative L1 transfer trap on national examinations. Option B is correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Congratulate' (እንኳዕ ሓጎሰካ ምባል) ዝብል ግሲ ወግዒ ወትሩ ምስ 'on' ዝብል መስተዋድድ ጥራይ እዩ ዝስዕብ (congratulate on - Option B)። ተማሃሮ 'ብምሓለፍካ' ንምባል 'for' (Option A) ብምጥቃም ክጋገዩ ይረኣዩ እዮም፤ እዚ ግን ዓቢ ናይ ምስግጋር ቋንቋ ጌጋ እዩ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Aster has always been exceptionally clever ________ mathematics and chemistry, which is why she wants to study engineering.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Adjectives describing skill or proficiency (like *good, bad, clever, expert*) must strictly be paired with the preposition 'at' ($$\text{clever} + \text{at} + \text{subject}$$).
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'in' (Option A) because they translate the Tigrinya locative prefix 'ኣብ' (in math) directly into English.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Aster has always been exceptionally clever ________ mathematics and chemistry, which is why she wants to study engineering.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Adjectives describing skill or proficiency (like *good, bad, clever, expert*) must strictly be paired with the preposition 'at' ($$\text{clever} + \text{at} + \text{subject}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'in' (Option A) because they translate the Tigrinya locative prefix 'ኣብ' (in math) directly into English. Option B 'at' is correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ናይ ክእለትን በላሕነትን መግለጺታት (good, clever, bad) ወትሩ ምስ 'at' ዝብል መስተዋድድ ጥራይ እዮም ዝስዕቡ (clever at - Option B)። ተማሃሮ ነቲ 'ኣብ ሒሳብ ጎበዝ እዩ' ዝብል ናይ ትግርኛ መዋቕር ብምቕዳሕ 'clever in' ክብሉ ይጋገዩ እዮም።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: The regional government is trying to find a viable solution ________ the severe water shortage in our town.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Nouns representing entries, answers, or solutions (like *solution, key, answer, response*) strictly require the preposition 'to' ($$\text{solution} + \text{to} + \text{noun}$$).
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'of' (Option A) because they translate possessive phrases like 'ናይዚ ጸገም መፍትሕ' (the key of this problem) directly, resulting in the incorrect use of 'of'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The regional government is trying to find a viable solution ________ the severe water shortage in our town.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Nouns representing entries, answers, or solutions (like *solution, key, answer, response*) strictly require the preposition 'to' ($$\text{solution} + \text{to} + \text{noun}$$).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'of' (Option A) because they translate possessive phrases like 'ናይዚ ጸገም መፍትሕ' (the key of this problem) directly, resulting in the incorrect use of 'of'. Option B is correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Solution' (መፍትሒ) ዝብል ስም ወትሩ ድሕሪኡ 'to' ዝብል መስተዋድድ እዩ ዝወስድ (solution to the problem - Option B)። 'of' ምጥቃም ናይ ትግርኛ 'ናይ...' ዝብል መዋቕር ቀጥታዊ ትርጉም ስለ ዝኾነ ሰዋስዋዊ ጌጋ ይፈጥር።

cards.title: Collocations, Idiomatic Expressions
rule: Collocations, Idiomatic Expressions & Similes

Definition: Collocations, Idiomatic Expressions & Similes (ልሙዳት ጥርኑፋት ቃላት፡ ምሳልያዊ ኣዘራርባታትን ምስላዊ ምንጽጻርን) are the lexical systems governing natural word pairings (collocations), non-literal figurative expressions (idioms), and vivid comparative templates (similes) used to achieve native-like fluency and descriptive precision in English.

Collocations (ልሙዳት ጥርኑፋት ቃላት) are the habitual, natural combinations of words in English. These pairings are not governed by logical grammatical rules, but by linguistic convention ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Noun}$$, e.g., *commit a crime* [ገበን ምፍጻም], not *do a crime*). A prime matriculation target is the distinction between do ($$\text{do} + \text{tasks/work}$$) and make ($$\text{make} + \text{creation/result}$$).

body: Collocations, Idiomatic Expressions & Similes

Definition: Collocations, Idiomatic Expressions & Similes (ልሙዳት ጥርኑፋት ቃላት፡ ምሳልያዊ ኣዘራርባታትን ምስላዊ ምንጽጻርን) are the lexical systems governing natural word pairings (collocations), non-literal figurative expressions (idioms), and vivid comparative templates (similes) used to achieve native-like fluency and descriptive precision in English.

Collocations (ልሙዳት ጥርኑፋት ቃላት) are the habitual, natural combinations of words in English. These pairings are not governed by logical grammatical rules, but by linguistic convention ($$\text{Verb} + \text{Noun}$$, e.g., *commit a crime* [ገበን ምፍጻም], not *do a crime*). A prime matriculation target is the distinction between do ($$\text{do} + \text{tasks/work}$$) and make ($$\text{make} + \text{creation/result}$$).

Other high-yield verbal collocations include *pay attention* ($$\text{pay} + \text{attention}$$, not *give*), *take an exam* (not *give* or *write*), and *keep a promise* (not *save*). Adjectival collocations such as *heavy rain* (not *strong rain*) and *fast food* (not *quick food*) are also frequently tested. For instance, the literal translation from Tigrinya "ሓያል ዝናብ" (strong rain) causes students to write "strong rain" instead of the natural English collocation *heavy rain*. Understanding these fixed pairings is essential for passing the language focus sections of the national exam.

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: The school board decided to ________ progress on the new laboratory construction project.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The noun 'progress' requires the verb 'make' to form the standard English collocation: $$\text{make} + \text{progress}$$.
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'do' (Option A) because they translate 'ዕብየት ገይሮም' (made progress) directly using the Tigrinya verb 'ገበረ' (to do).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The school board decided to ________ progress on the new laboratory construction project.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The noun 'progress' requires the verb 'make' to form the standard English collocation: $$\text{make} + \text{progress}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'do' (Option A) because they translate 'ዕብየት ገይሮም' (made progress) directly using the Tigrinya verb 'ገበረ' (to do). Option B 'make' is correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Progress' (ዕብየት/ምስጓም) ዝብል ስም ምስ 'make' ዝብል ግሲ ጥራይ እዩ ዝጣመር (make progress - Option B)። ተማሃሮ 'ዕብየት ገይሩ' ንምባል 'do progress' ክብሉ ይጋገዩ እዮም፤ እዚ ግን ናይ ቀጥታዊ ትርጉም መጻወድያ እዩ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Because of the ________ rain, the regional football championship was postponed until next week.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The noun 'rain' is modified by the adjective 'heavy' to describe high volume, forming the fixed collocation: $$\text{heavy} + \text{rain}$$.
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'strong' (Option A) because they translate 'ሓያል ዝናብ' (strong rain) directly from Tigrinya.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Because of the ________ rain, the regional football championship was postponed until next week.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The noun 'rain' is modified by the adjective 'heavy' to describe high volume, forming the fixed collocation: $$\text{heavy} + \text{rain}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'strong' (Option A) because they translate 'ሓያል ዝናብ' (strong rain) directly from Tigrinya. In English, 'strong' is used for wind, while 'heavy' is strictly used for rain. Option B is correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ምስ 'rain' (ዝናብ) ዝኸይድ ናይ መጠን መግለጺ ቃል 'heavy' ጥራይ እዩ (heavy rain - Option B - ከቢድ ዝናብ)። ኣብ ትግርኛ 'ሓያል ዝናብ' ስለ ዝበሃል፡ ተማሃሮ 'strong rain' ብምባል ክጋገዩ ይረኣዩ እዮም፤ እዚ ግን ጌጋ ጥምረት እዩ።

units.intro: Grammar from Study Notes ch.19: Synonyms, Antonyms, Analogies & One-Word Substitutes.

cards.title: Synonyms, Antonyms, Analogies
rule: Synonyms, Antonyms, Analogies & One-Word Substitutes

Definition: Vocabulary Relations and Semantic Matching (ስነ-ትርጉማዊ ዝምድናታትን ምትካእ ቃላትን) refers to the systems of identifying words with similar meanings (synonyms), opposite meanings (antonyms), proportional logical relationships (analogies), and single lexical terms that compress complex descriptive definitions (one-word substitutes).

In national matriculation examinations, vocabulary is heavily tested through context-based semantic matching. Words rarely possess absolute synonyms; instead, their closest semantic partner is determined entirely by the surrounding clausal syntax ($$\text{Word} \leftrightarrow \text{Contextual Synonym}$$). Academic English relies extensively on Greek and Latin roots (e.g., *mal-* [bad], *bene-* [good], *chron-* [time], *auto-* [self]). Contrast this with Tigrinya's Semitic root-and-pattern morphology, where related vocabulary is derived internally from consonantal roots (ሰለስተ-ፊደል ሱር). Because English utilizes concatenative foreign roots (e.g., *benevolent* $$\rightarrow$$ *well-wishing*), Tigrinya speakers must learn to dissect complex academic words into their constituent morphemes ($$\text{Prefix} + \text{Root} + \text{Suffix}$$) to deduce synonyms and antonyms without relying on rote memorization.

body: Synonyms, Antonyms, Analogies & One-Word Substitutes

Definition: Vocabulary Relations and Semantic Matching (ስነ-ትርጉማዊ ዝምድናታትን ምትካእ ቃላትን) refers to the systems of identifying words with similar meanings (synonyms), opposite meanings (antonyms), proportional logical relationships (analogies), and single lexical terms that compress complex descriptive definitions (one-word substitutes).

In national matriculation examinations, vocabulary is heavily tested through context-based semantic matching. Words rarely possess absolute synonyms; instead, their closest semantic partner is determined entirely by the surrounding clausal syntax ($$\text{Word} \leftrightarrow \text{Contextual Synonym}$$). Academic English relies extensively on Greek and Latin roots (e.g., *mal-* [bad], *bene-* [good], *chron-* [time], *auto-* [self]). Contrast this with Tigrinya's Semitic root-and-pattern morphology, where related vocabulary is derived internally from consonantal roots (ሰለስተ-ፊደል ሱር). Because English utilizes concatenative foreign roots (e.g., *benevolent* $$\rightarrow$$ *well-wishing*), Tigrinya speakers must learn to dissect complex academic words into their constituent morphemes ($$\text{Prefix} + \text{Root} + \text{Suffix}$$) to deduce synonyms and antonyms without relying on rote memorization.

Antonyms (ኣንጻር ቃላት) are tested both as entirely distinct lexical items (e.g., *ephemeral* vs. *permanent*) and as morphological opposites formed via negative prefixes ($$\text{Root} \leftrightarrow \text{Prefix} + \text{Root}$$, e.g., *orthodox* vs. *unorthodox*, *compatible* vs. *incompatible*). In reading passages, contextual clues such as contrastive conjunctions (*however, although, on the other hand, whereas*) serve as semantic signposts pointing directly to the required antonymous meaning. Students must look for these structural transitions to accurately determine the opposite meaning of a highlighted word.
