cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: The effects of the traditional medicine were ________, lasting only a few minutes before the pain returned.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The context 'lasting only a few minutes' indicates that the effects were short-lived, requiring an adjective meaning temporary.
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often confuse 'potent' (powerful) or 'inevitable' (unavoidable) with the correct option.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The effects of the traditional medicine were ________, lasting only a few minutes before the pain returned.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The context 'lasting only a few minutes' indicates that the effects were short-lived, requiring an adjective meaning temporary.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often confuse 'potent' (powerful) or 'inevitable' (unavoidable) with the correct option. 'Ephemeral' (Option B) is the precise academic synonym for short-lived.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Ephemeral' (ሳሕቲ/ኣዝዩ ሕጽር ዝበለ ግዜ ዝጸንሕ) ዝብል ቃል፡ ንሓጺር እዋን ጥራይ ዝጸንሕ ኩነታት ንምግላጽ የገልግል። እቲ ሓረግ 'lasting only a few minutes' (ንሒደት ደቓይቕ ጥራይ ዝጸንሐ) ስለ ዝበለ፡ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option B እዩ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Unlike his highly ________ predecessor, the new director was malevolent and treated the employees with cruelty.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The contrastive conjunction 'Unlike' indicates that the blank must contain the antonym of 'malevolent' (evil-wishing/cruel).
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students must identify 'benevolent' (Option B - kind/well-wishing) as the exact antonym of 'malevolent'.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Unlike his highly ________ predecessor, the new director was malevolent and treated the employees with cruelty.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The contrastive conjunction 'Unlike' indicates that the blank must contain the antonym of 'malevolent' (evil-wishing/cruel).

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students must identify 'benevolent' (Option B - kind/well-wishing) as the exact antonym of 'malevolent'. Both words share the root '-volent' (wishing), with 'bene-' (good) and 'male-' (bad) prefixes.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'Unlike' (ዘይከም) ዝብል ናይ መነጻጸሪ ቃል ስለ ዘሎ፡ እቲ ባዶ ቦታ ናይ 'malevolent' (እኩይ/ጨካን) ኣንጻር ቃል ክኸውን ኣለዎ። 'Benevolent' (ርሕሩሕ/ደግ) ምስቲ 'bene-' (ጽቡቕ) ዝብል ናይ ላቲን ሱር ዝተኣሳሰር ኮይኑ ቅኑዕ ኣንጻር ቃል እዩ (Option B)።

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Choose the option that correctly completes the analogy: **Carpenter : Saw :: Surgeon : ________**
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The relationship is Worker-and-Tool ($$\text{Worker} : \text{Tool}$$). A carpenter uses a saw as his primary tool, in the same way that a surgeon uses a scalpel as his primary tool.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'Operation' (Option D) or 'Hospital' (Option B) because they are related to surgery, but they do not match the specific Worker-and-Tool logical relationship. Option C is correct.

cards.title: Conversational English, Dialogue Completion
rule: Conversational English, Dialogue Completion & Social Expressions

Definition: Conversational English and Social Expressions (ናይ ዝርርብ እንግሊዘኛን ተግባራዊ ማሕበራዊ መግለጺታትን) are the pragmatic and functional linguistic formulas used to navigate situational interactions — such as advising, complaining, inviting, agreeing, and expressing sympathy — in accordance with standard English social conventions.

Conversational English is a major section of national examinations, designed to assess a candidate's communicative competence in various social and situational contexts. Dialogue completion (ምስምማዕ ዘረባታት) evaluates how well candidates can match conversational turns by selecting expressions that align with standard social expectations. Unlike formal written grammar, conversational English prioritizes pragmatic appropriateness over mere grammatical accuracy. Tigrinya speakers often face difficulties here because social formulas in Tigrinya are deeply rooted in Semitic cultural codes, which do not translate directly to English. Direct literal translation of Tigrinya polite expressions can sound grammatically correct but pragmatically bizarre or rude in English, making this a high-yield exam filter.

cards.title: Notes
body: Conversational English, Dialogue Completion & Social Expressions

Definition: Conversational English and Social Expressions (ናይ ዝርርብ እንግሊዘኛን ተግባራዊ ማሕበራዊ መግለጺታትን) are the pragmatic and functional linguistic formulas used to navigate situational interactions — such as advising, complaining, inviting, agreeing, and expressing sympathy — in accordance with standard English social conventions.

Conversational English is a major section of national examinations, designed to assess a candidate's communicative competence in various social and situational contexts. Dialogue completion (ምስምማዕ ዘረባታት) evaluates how well candidates can match conversational turns by selecting expressions that align with standard social expectations. Unlike formal written grammar, conversational English prioritizes pragmatic appropriateness over mere grammatical accuracy. Tigrinya speakers often face difficulties here because social formulas in Tigrinya are deeply rooted in Semitic cultural codes, which do not translate directly to English. Direct literal translation of Tigrinya polite expressions can sound grammatically correct but pragmatically bizarre or rude in English, making this a high-yield exam filter.

Expressions of strong agreement are frequent targets on national examinations. Key formulas include I couldn't agree more! (ፈጺመ እሰማማዕ እየ) and You can say that again! (ብምሉእ ሓሳብካ እሰማማዕ እየ). Tigrinya speakers often misinterpret *I couldn't agree more!* as a negative statement of disagreement due to the modal auxiliary *couldn't* ($$\text{couldn't} \rightarrow \text{Disagreement?}$$). In standard English, however, it represents the highest level of agreement. Similarly, *You can say that again!* is a fixed idiomatic phrase showing strong agreement, not a literal request to the speaker to repeat their words. Translating these expressions literally into Tigrinya leads to major comprehension errors during exam tasks.

head: Social Function

ብምሉእ ሓሳብካ እሰማማዕ እየ (Strong positive agreement)
*I'd love to, but I have an exam.*
ደስ ምበለኒ ነይሩ ግን ... (Appreciate + Decline + Reason)
*If I were you, I would study.* / *Why don't you...?*
*I'm sorry to hear that.* / *What a pity!*

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem:
Speaker A: 'The new school principal is exceptionally supportive and fair.'
Speaker B: '________ He has already resolved several student complaints.'

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Speaker A makes a positive statement.
Speaker B's following sentence ('He has already resolved...') confirms strong agreement.
We need a standard expression of strong agreement.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Speaker A: 'The new school principal is exceptionally supportive and fair.'
Speaker B: '________ He has already resolved several student complaints.'
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Speaker A makes a positive statement. Speaker B's following sentence ('He has already resolved...') confirms strong agreement. We need a standard expression of strong agreement.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often avoid 'I couldn't agree more!' (Option A) because they see the negative modal 'couldn't' and assume it means disagreement. This is a classic pragmatic trap. In English, 'I couldn't agree more!' means complete agreement.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
Speaker A 'እቲ ርእሰ-መምህር ንፉዕ እዩ' ኢሉ ሓሳቡ ክገልጽ ከሎ፡ Speaker B ድማ 'ብምሉእ ሓሳብካ እሰማማዕ እየ' ክብል ይደሊ ኣሎ (እቲ ዝሰዓበ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ነዚ የረጋግጽ)። ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ፍጹም ስምምዕ ንምግላጽ 'I couldn't agree more!' (Option A - ካብዚ ንላዕሊ ክሰማማዕ ኣይክእልን/ምሉእ ብምሉእ እሰማማዕ) ንጥቀም።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem:
Speaker A: 'Would you like to attend the graduation party at our house tonight?'
Speaker B: '________ I have to complete my biology assignment before tomorrow.'

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Speaker A extends an invitation.
Speaker B provides a reason for declining ('I have to complete my assignment...').
This requires a polite refusal formula: $$\text{Appreciation} + \text{but} + \text{Reason}$$.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Speaker A: 'Would you like to attend the graduation party at our house tonight?'
Speaker B: '________ I have to complete my biology assignment before tomorrow.'

options.D: I am sorry to hear that,

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Speaker A extends an invitation. Speaker B provides a reason for declining ('I have to complete my assignment...'). This requires a polite refusal formula: $$\text{Appreciation} + \text{but} + \text{Reason}$$.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Option A is too direct and impolite. Option C accepts but contradicts the following clause. Option B 'I'd love to, but' is the correct polite refusal formula.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ዕድመ ብትሕትና ንምእባይ (polite refusal) እንጥቀመሉ ናይ ዝርርብ ቀመር 'I'd love to, but...' (Option B - ደስ ምበለኒ ነይሩ ግን...) እዩ። 'No, I don't want to' (Option A) ምጥቃም ግን ብባህሊ እንግሊዘኛ ዘይልሙድን ብዕሉግን ተገይሩ እዩ ዝውሰድ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem:
Speaker A: 'I am so confused about which engineering field to study at university.'
Speaker B: '________ consult the academic counselor before making a final decision?'

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The blank is followed by a base verb 'consult' and ends with a question mark.
This requires the suggestion formula: $$\text{Why don't you} + \text{V}_{\text{base}} \dots ?$$
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Speaker A: 'I am so confused about which engineering field to study at university.'
Speaker B: '________ consult the academic counselor before making a final decision?'

options.B: If I were you, I would

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
The blank is followed by a base verb 'consult' and ends with a question mark. This requires the suggestion formula: $$\text{Why don't you} + \text{V}_{\text{base}} \dots ?$$

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Option B lacks the question format. Option C 'You'd better to' incorrectly inserts 'to' after 'better'. Option A 'Why don't you' is syntactically and pragmatically correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
እቲ ባዶ ቦታ ዝስዕቦ ግሲ 'consult' (base verb) ኮይኑ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ድማ ብሕቶ ምልክት ይውዳእ። ምስዚ መዋቕር ዝኸይድ ናይ ምኽሪ ሓረግ 'Why don't you' (Option A - ስለምንታይ ዘይትገብር?) እዩ። 'If I were you' (Option B) ሕቶ ምልክት ኣይወስድን እዩ።

cards.title: Pronunciation, Vowel Sounds
rule: Pronunciation, Vowel Sounds & Silent Letters

Definition: English Phonology and Orthography (ናይ እንግሊዘኛ ድምጽታትን ኣደማምጻ ቃላትን) refers to the study of spelling-to-sound correspondences, including the identification of silent letters, vowel sound differentiation (short vs. long vowels), consonant digraphs, and rules of word stress, which are heavily tested in "Odd One Out" national exam formats.

In English, there is a significant divergence between spelling (orthography) and pronunciation (phonology). English is not a phonetic language; the same alphabetical spelling can produce completely different phonetic sounds (e.g., the spelling 'ough' in *cough, tough, though, through*). In contrast, Tigrinya's Ge'ez script (ፊደል) is strictly phonetic: each written symbol represents a single, highly consistent consonant-vowel syllable, and every written letter is voiced. Consequently, Tigrinya speakers instinctively attempt to pronounce every written English letter, leading to persistent pronunciation errors. This spelling-to-sound transfer is heavily targeted in "Odd One Out" (ፍሉይ ድምጺ ምልላይ) sections of national matriculation exams.

units.intro: Grammar from Study Notes ch.23: Reading Comprehension, Context Clues & Reference Words.

cards.title: Reading Comprehension, Context Clues
rule: Reading Comprehension, Context Clues & Reference Words

Definition: Reading Comprehension & Reference tracking (ናይ ምንባብን ምግንዛብን ክእለት) refers to the cognitive strategies of skimming for main ideas, scanning for specific details, using surrounding semantic context clues to decode unfamiliar vocabulary, and tracing reference words (pronouns and determiners) to their correct nouns or clausal antecedents.

Reading comprehension is a critical component of the national matriculation examination, accounting for a significant portion of the total English score. Successful reading requires mastering skimming (ብላዕሊ ላዕሊ ምንባብ) and scanning (ሰሊኽካ ፍሉይ ሓበሬታ ምድላይ). Skimming ($$\text{Skimming} \rightarrow \text{Main Idea / Title}$$) is the rapid reading of introductory and concluding paragraphs, along with topic sentences, to grasp the general theme of a passage. Scanning ($$\text{Scanning} \rightarrow \text{Specific details / Names / Dates}$$) involves moving one's eyes rapidly over the text to locate specific keywords, dates, or figures without reading every word. Tigrinya speakers often struggle with reading speed because they perform subvocalization (ብውሽጢ ምድማጽ) or mental translation (ብኣእምሮ ምትርጓም), which slows down their processing. Students must train themselves to bypass word-by-word translation to improve their reading efficiency.

Students must train themselves to bypass word-by-word translation to improve their reading efficiency.

Deducing the meaning of unfamiliar words using context clues (ኩነታዊ ትርጉም ምፍላይ) is a highly valued exam skill. Examiners frequently underline difficult academic words in passages and ask for their closest meaning. Students can use four types of context clues: - Synonym clues: the text provides a similar word nearby. - Antonym/Contrast clues: the text uses contrast markers like *however, although, whereas* ($$\text{Unfamiliar Word} + \text{Contrast Marker} \rightarrow \text{Antonym Clue}$$).

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q:
Read the context and answer the question:
'The ministry launched a new educational portal last week. **It** was designed to provide free learning modules for high school students.'
The pronoun 'It' refers to:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
'It' is a singular neuter subject pronoun. Its antecedent must be a singular inanimate noun phrase mentioned in the preceding sentence.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students might choose 'the ministry' (singular) or 'free learning modules' (plural). By applying the Pronoun Substitution Test ('The new educational portal was designed to...'), Option B is clearly correct.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
'It' (ንሱ - ዘይህይወታዊ ነጸላ) ዝብል ተውላጠ ስም ንሓደ ቅድሚኡ ዝተገልጸ ነጸላ ስም እዩ ዝውክል። ነቲ ሓረግ 'The new educational portal was designed...' (እቲ ሓድሽ መርበብ ሓበሬታ...) ኢልና ክንተክኦ ከለና ግቡእ ትርጉም ስለ ዝህብ፡ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option B እዩ።

cards.title: Common Grammatical Mistakes
rule: Common Grammatical Mistakes & L1 Interference Traps

Definition: L1 Interference and Grammatical Errors (ናይ ቀዳማይ ቋንቋ ጽልዋን ስሩዓት ሰዋስዋዊ ጌጋታትን) refers to the systematic syntactic, morphological, and orthographic errors made by Tigrinya-native speakers due to the negative transfer of Semitic linguistic structures and phonology into English.

Negative language transfer (ኣሉታዊ ምስግጋር ቋንቋ) occurs when the grammar, phonology, or word order of a student's native language conflicts with the rules of the target language. Since Tigrinya is a highly inflected Subject-Object-Verb ($$\text{S-O-V}$$) Semitic language, and English is an analytical Subject-Verb-Object ($$\text{S-V-O}$$) Germanic language, Tigrinya speakers face systematic, predictable interference traps. Rather than treating these errors as random, uncoordinated mistakes, this chapter provides a systematic diagnostic framework to identify, analyze, and neutralize these traps, helping students secure maximum marks on national matriculation examinations.

cards.title: Notes
body: Common Grammatical Mistakes & L1 Interference Traps

Definition: L1 Interference and Grammatical Errors (ናይ ቀዳማይ ቋንቋ ጽልዋን ስሩዓት ሰዋስዋዊ ጌጋታትን) refers to the systematic syntactic, morphological, and orthographic errors made by Tigrinya-native speakers due to the negative transfer of Semitic linguistic structures and phonology into English.

Negative language transfer (ኣሉታዊ ምስግጋር ቋንቋ) occurs when the grammar, phonology, or word order of a student's native language conflicts with the rules of the target language. Since Tigrinya is a highly inflected Subject-Object-Verb ($$\text{S-O-V}$$) Semitic language, and English is an analytical Subject-Verb-Object ($$\text{S-V-O}$$) Germanic language, Tigrinya speakers face systematic, predictable interference traps. Rather than treating these errors as random, uncoordinated mistakes, this chapter provides a systematic diagnostic framework to identify, analyze, and neutralize these traps, helping students secure maximum marks on national matriculation examinations.

A prominent syntax error is the Redundant Double Subject ($$\times \text{Subject Noun} + \text{Subject Pronoun} + \text{Verb}$$). In Tigrinya, verbs are conjugated with obligatorily embedded pronominal subject markers (e.g., "ኣቦይ ሓረስታይ [ንሱ] እዩ"). This structure makes native speakers feel that stating the noun subject ("My father") requires immediate pronoun reinforcement ("he") before the verb, resulting in ungrammatical sentences like "My father *he* is a hardworking farmer." In standard English, a clause must strictly contain only a single subject referent per verb; therefore, writing "My father is a hardworking farmer" is the only correct form.

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct and free from L1 double-subject errors?

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
In English, a clause must contain only a single subject referent per verb.
The noun phrase 'My elder brother' is the subject of 'is studying'.
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**

cards.answer: My elder brother is studying civil engineering at university.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following sentences is grammatically correct and free from L1 double-subject errors?

options.A: My elder brother he is studying civil engineering at university.
options.B: My elder brother is studying civil engineering at university.
options.C: My elder brother, he is studying civil engineering at university.
options.D: My elder brother him is studying civil engineering at university.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
In English, a clause must contain only a single subject referent per verb. The noun phrase 'My elder brother' is the subject of 'is studying'.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Options A and C contain a redundant pronoun 'he' immediately following the noun subject. This is a classic double-subject error caused by Tigrinya verb conjugation habits. Option B correctly eliminates the redundant pronoun.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ ወግዒ ሓደ ምሉእ ሓሳብ ሓደ ዋና ባእታ (Subject) ጥራይ እዩ ዝወስድ። 'My elder brother' (ሓወይ) ባዕሉ እኹል ዋና ባእታ ስለ ዝኾነ፡ ድሕሪኡ 'he' (ንሱ) ምጥቃም ድርብ ዋና ባእታ (Double Subject) ዝበሃል ዓቢ ጌጋ ይፈጥር። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option B እዩ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Because the physics laboratory was locked yesterday afternoon, ________ we were unable to perform the experiment.

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
'Because' is a subordinating conjunction at the beginning of the sentence to connect the clauses.
In English, only one conjunction can connect two clauses; adding a second is a double-conjunction error.
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Because the physics laboratory was locked yesterday afternoon, ________ we were unable to perform the experiment.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
'Because' is a subordinating conjunction at the beginning of the sentence to connect the clauses. In English, only one conjunction can connect two clauses; adding a second is a double-conjunction error.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
Students often choose 'so' (Option A) because in Tigrinya, it is natural to pair cause with result (e.g., 'ስለ ዝሓመመ፡ ስለዚ...'). Option D is correct because no extra connector is allowed.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ኣብ መጀመርታ እቲ ምሉእ ሓሳብ 'Because' (ምኽንያቱ/ስለ ዝ-) ዝብል መተሓሓዚ ስለ ዘሎ፡ ኣብቲ ካልኣይ ሓረግ 'so' (ስለዚ) ምጥቃም ዓቢ ናይ ድርብ መስተጻምር ጌጋ (double-conjunction error) ይፈጥር። ስለዚ ቅኑዕ መልሲ Option D ([No connector] - ዋላ ሓደ ቃል ኣየድልይን) እዩ።

cards.title: Worked practice
cards.problem: Identify the sentence that contains a copula verb omission error caused by L1 interference:

steps.text: **Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Every English sentence expressing a state of being requires an explicit copula verb ('is', 'are', 'was', 'were') between the subject and the adjective complement.
**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
In Option C, the copula verb 'is' is completely missing.

cards.answer: My brother very hardworking and always studies late.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Identify the sentence that contains a copula verb omission error caused by L1 interference:

options.A: She is an exceptionally clever student in our class.
options.B: They are from the southern region of Eritrea.
options.C: My brother very hardworking and always studies late.
options.D: We were delighted to receive your invitation.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the grammatical structure**
Every English sentence expressing a state of being requires an explicit copula verb ('is', 'are', 'was', 'were') between the subject and the adjective complement.

**Step 2: Identify the matriculation trap**
In Option C, the copula verb 'is' is completely missing. In Tigrinya, the copula can sometimes be omitted in speech, leading students to translate directly as 'My brother very hardworking...', which is incorrect. Option C is the target error.

**Step 3: Tigrinya Explanation (ትርጉም)**
ኣብ እንግሊዘኛ 'ምዃን' ዘመልክቱ ሓገዝቲ ግሶች (copula verbs - is, are) ወግዒ ክጸሓፉ ኣለዎም። ኣብ Option C 'My brother [is] very hardworking' ክኸውን ስለ ዝነበሮ፡ እቲ ግሲ ብምጥፋኡ ጌጋ ኣለዎ። ተማሃሮ ብስሕተት 'My brother very...' ኢሎም ክጽሕፉ ይረኣዩ እዮም።

options.C: My elder brother, he is studying civil engineering at university.
options.D: My elder brother him is studying civil engineering at university.

why: Answer B: My elder brother is studying civil engineering at university.
In English, a clause must contain only a single subject referent per verb. The noun phrase 'My elder brother' is the subject of 'is studying'.

questions.q: Because the physics laboratory was locked yesterday afternoon, ________ we were unable to perform the experiment.
questions.label: 2. Because the physics laboratory was locked yesterday afternoo
why: 'Because' is a subordinating conjunction at the beginning of the sentence to connect the clauses. In English, only one conjunction can connect two clauses; adding a second is a double-conjunction error.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: Identify the sentence that contains a copula verb omission error caused by L1 interference:
questions.label: 3. Identify the sentence that contains a copula verb omission e

options.A: She is an exceptionally clever student in our class.
options.B: They are from the southern region of Eritrea.
options.C: My brother very hardworking and always studies late.
options.D: We were delighted to receive your invitation.

why: Answer C: My brother very hardworking and always studies late.
Every English sentence expressing a state of being requires an explicit copula verb ('is', 'are', 'was', 'were') between the subject and the adjective complement.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: The program coordinator congratulated the candidates ________ achieving top scores on the ESSLCE.
questions.label: 4. The program coordinator congratulated the candidates _______
why: The verb 'congratulate' strictly requires the preposition 'on' followed by a noun or gerund: $$\text{congratulate} + \text{someone} + \text{on} + \text{something}$$.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: The administrative assistant provided us with many useful ________ regarding the registration process.
questions.label: 5. The administrative assistant provided us with many useful __
why: 'Advice' is strictly uncountable and cannot be pluralized with an '-s' suffix. To express plurality, we must use partitive phrases like 'pieces of advice'.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: Identify the sentence that displays correct pronoun placement for a separable phrasal verb:
questions.label: 6. Identify the sentence that displays correct pronoun placemen

options.A: Please turn off the light before you leave.
options.B: Please turn the light off before you leave.
options.C: Please turn it off before you leave.
options.D: Please turn off it before you leave.

why: Answer D: Please turn off it before you leave.

'Turn off' is a transitive separable phrasal verb. Noun objects can go in the middle or at the end. Pronoun objects ('it') **must** go in the middle: $$\text{Verb} + \text{Pronoun} + \text{Particle}$$.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: The chemistry instructor told the students ________ any of the chemical solutions.
questions.label: 7. The chemistry instructor told the students ________ any of t
why: This is a reported negative command. Negative commands are reported using the structure: $$\text{reporting verb} + \text{object} + \text{not to} + \text{V}_{\text{base}}$$.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: Choose the sentence that displays correct English word order ($$\text{S-V-O}$$):
questions.label: 8. Choose the sentence that displays correct English word order

options.A: The doctor the patient examined yesterday afternoon.
options.B: The doctor examined the patient yesterday afternoon.
options.C: Yesterday afternoon the doctor the patient examined.
options.D: Examined the doctor the patient yesterday afternoon.

why: Answer B: The doctor examined the patient yesterday afternoon.
English requires a strict Subject-Verb-Object ($$\text{S-V-O}$$) pattern. The subject is 'The doctor', the verb is 'examined', and the direct object is 'the patient'.
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

questions.q: When I was a young boy living in the village, I was extremely afraid ________ wild dogs.
questions.label: 9. When I was a young boy living in the village, I was extremel
why: The adjective 'afraid' must strictly be paired with the preposition 'of' ($$\text{afraid} + \text{of} + \text{noun}$$).
questions.tip: Eliminate options that break the grammar rule first.

why: Answer B: We had a delicious lunch in the school dining room.
The verb 'dine' ends in a single silent 'e'. When adding the suffix '-ing', the 'e' is dropped to form 'dining' (/ˈdaɪnɪŋ/).
